questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man with a history of IV drug use presents with fatigue, nausea, and mild jaundice. He reports a history of similar symptoms about 5 years ago, which resolved spontaneously. Laboratory testing shows elevated liver enzymes, and an ELISA test is positive for anti-HCV antibodies. Which of the following tests would be most appropriate to confirm an active HCV infection in this patient?
questions.solution: HCV is an RNA virus and best test for any RNA viruses is RT-PCR. Laboratory Diagnosis: Molecular Methods (RT-PCR): Gold standard for confirming active infection; detects HCV RNA 2–3 weeks post-infection, used for viral load, treatment response, and genotype. (Option C) Antibody Detection Tests: ELISA is standard for initial screening with high sensitivity and specificity. Cannot differentiate active vs. past infections. HCV Core Antigen Assay: Automated, cost-effective for active infection diagnosis and treatment monitoring. Less sensitive than RT-PCR. (Option A) Biopsy (Option B) is the gold standard for staging Fibroscan (Option D) is a non-invasive alternative for assessing liver fibrosis. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
HCV is an RNA virus and best test for any RNA viruses is RT-PCR.

Laboratory Diagnosis:

  • Molecular Methods (RT-PCR): Gold standard for confirming active infection; detects HCV RNA 2–3 weeks post-infection, used for viral load, treatment response, and genotype. (Option C)
  • Antibody Detection Tests: ELISA is standard for initial screening with high sensitivity and specificity. Cannot differentiate active vs. past infections.
  • HCV Core Antigen Assay: Automated, cost-effective for active infection diagnosis and treatment monitoring. Less sensitive than RT-PCR. (Option A)
  • Biopsy (Option B) is the gold standard for staging
  • Fibroscan (Option D) is a non-invasive alternative for assessing liver fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient presents with recurrent infections and a history of autoimmune disease. Laboratory tests reveal a deficiency in complement component C3. Which of the following is the most likely consequence of this deficiency?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old patient presents with recurrent infections and a history of autoimmune disease. Laboratory tests reveal a deficiency in complement component C3. Which of the following is the most likely consequence of this deficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased susceptibility to infections by Neisseria meningitidis

options.label: B
options.text: Impaired opsonization and phagocytosis, leading to severe bacterial infections

options.label: D
options.text: Enhanced immune complex clearance and reduced inflammation

questions.answerText: Impaired opsonization and phagocytosis, leading to severe bacterial infections
questions.solution: 777195ea42ef0356">phagocytosis due to C3 deficiency increases susceptibility to severe bacterial infections, particularly from pyogenic bacteria. Complement Deficiency arise from genetic defects in complement components or regulatory proteins, compromising both innate and acquired immunity. Consequences of Complement Deficiency: Impaired immune clearance → poor removal of antigens/immune complexes Recurrent infections : Especially bacterial/fungal (C3 deficiency) – pneumonia, skin infections, sepsis Neisserial infections : C5–C9 deficiency → meningitis, septicaemia, gonorrhoea Autoimmune disease : SLE from immune complex deposition and tissue inflammation Specific Deficiencies and Associated Syndromes: Deficiency Condition/Clinical Manifestation C1 Inhibitor Deficiency (Option C ruled out) Hereditary angioneurotic oedema: Uncontrolled activation of classical pathway causes episodic swelling (can be life-threatening). C3 Deficiency Increased susceptibility to severe recurrent pyogenic infections; impaired opsonization, phagocytosis, and immune complex clearance. C5-C9 Deficiencies Increased susceptibility to bacteraemia, especially with Gram-negative diplococci; impaired formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC). Enhanced immune complex clearance and reduced inflammation (option D) are incorrect, as C3 deficiency leads to impaired clearance and increased inflammation due to the accumulation of immune complexes. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
777195ea42ef0356">phagocytosis due to C3 deficiency increases susceptibility to severe bacterial infections, particularly from pyogenic bacteria.

Complement Deficiency arise from genetic defects in complement components or regulatory proteins, compromising both innate and acquired immunity.

Consequences of Complement Deficiency:

  • Impaired immune clearance → poor removal of antigens/immune complexes

  • Recurrent infections: Especially bacterial/fungal (C3 deficiency) – pneumonia, skin infections, sepsis

  • Neisserial infections: C5–C9 deficiency → meningitis, septicaemia, gonorrhoea

  • Autoimmune disease: SLE from immune complex deposition and tissue inflammation

Specific Deficiencies and Associated Syndromes:

Deficiency

Condition/Clinical Manifestation

C1 Inhibitor Deficiency (Option C ruled out)

Hereditary angioneurotic oedema: Uncontrolled activation of classical pathway causes episodic swelling (can be life-threatening).

C3 Deficiency

Increased susceptibility to severe recurrent pyogenic infections; impaired opsonization, phagocytosis, and immune complex clearance.

C5-C9 Deficiencies

Increased susceptibility to bacteraemia, especially with Gram-negative diplococci; impaired formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC).

 

Enhanced immune complex clearance and reduced inflammation (option D) are incorrect, as C3 deficiency leads to impaired clearance and increased inflammation due to the accumulation of immune complexes.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases exclusively involves obligate hosts in its transmission cycle?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following diseases exclusively involves obligate hosts in its transmission cycle?
questions.solution: Obligate hosts are the only hosts that are necessary for the completion of a pathogen's life cycle. Person-to-person transmission is present. E.g., Typhoid, Measles Sleeping sickness (Option B): Sleeping sickness (African trypanosomiasis) involves multiple hosts in its transmission cycle, not just obligate hosts. The cycle includes: Tsetse flies (vector) Humans (Main host for Trypanosoma brucei gambiense) Wild and domestic animals (Reservoir hosts for Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense). This complex cycle involves both obligate and non-obligate hosts. Hydatid disease (Option C): Hydatid disease is caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus. Definitive hosts: dogs and other canines Intermediate hosts: sheep, cattle, humans This cycle doesn't rely solely on obligate hosts. Filaria (Option D): Filariasis is caused by filarial worms (e.g., Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi). It involves multiple hosts in its transmission cycle: Mosquitoes (vector), Humans (main host) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• Obligate hosts are the only hosts that are necessary for the completion of a pathogen's life cycle.
  • Person-to-person transmission is present.
  • E.g., Typhoid, Measles

Sleeping sickness (Option B): Sleeping sickness (African trypanosomiasis) involves multiple hosts in its transmission cycle, not just obligate hosts. The cycle includes:

  • Tsetse flies (vector)
  • Humans (Main host for Trypanosoma brucei gambiense)
  • Wild and domestic animals (Reservoir hosts for Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense).
  • This complex cycle involves both obligate and non-obligate hosts.

 

Hydatid disease (Option C): Hydatid disease is caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus.

  • Definitive hosts: dogs and other canines
  • Intermediate hosts: sheep, cattle, humans This cycle doesn't rely solely on obligate hosts.

 

Filaria (Option D): Filariasis is caused by filarial worms (e.g., Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi). It involves multiple hosts in its transmission cycle: Mosquitoes (vector), Humans (main host)

questions.solution: customMeta" data-dictid="754ab07a2e1692777183ed178c883d">biopsy image is Mallory-Denk bodies , a hallmark of both alcohol-induced and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. These are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions seen in hepatocytes. They comprise intermediate filaments, primarily cytokeratin 8 and 18, and other proteins like ubiquitin. They indicate cellular injury and are often associated with hepatocyte ballooning and inflammation. Mallory - Denk bodies are also seen in (New Indian WATCH) N on alcoholic fatty liver disease Indian childhood cirrhosis W ilson’s disease A lcoholic liver disease T umors like hepatocellular carcinoma C hronic cholestasis Focal nodular H yperplasia Ground-glass hepatocytes (Option B): This morphological change is seen in chronic hepatitis B infection, where hepatocytes display a granular, homogenous eosinophilic cytoplasm due to the accumulation of HBsAg in the swollen smooth endoplasmic reticulum. Councilman bodies (Option C): Councilman bodies (or acidophilic bodies) are eosinophilic, round structures representing hepatocyte apoptosis. They are typically seen in acute viral hepatitis and indicate severe hepatocellular injury. Glycogenated hepatocytes (Option D): Glycogenated hepatocytes are hepatocytes with increased intracytoplasmic glycogen content. This finding is often seen in conditions associated with metabolic disturbances, such as glycogen storage diseases or acute fatty liver of pregnancy. @Neet_pg_bot

customMeta" data-dictid="754ab07a2e1692777183ed178c883d">biopsy image is Mallory-Denk bodies, a hallmark of both alcohol-induced and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.
  • These are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions seen in hepatocytes.
  • They comprise intermediate filaments, primarily cytokeratin 8 and 18, and other proteins like ubiquitin.
  • They indicate cellular injury and are often associated with hepatocyte ballooning and inflammation.

 

Mallory - Denk bodies are also seen in (New Indian WATCH)

  • Non alcoholic fatty liver disease
  • Indian childhood cirrhosis
  • Wilson’s disease
  • Alcoholic liver disease
  • Tumors like hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Chronic cholestasis
  • Focal nodular Hyperplasia


 

Ground-glass hepatocytes (Option B):

This morphological change is seen in chronic hepatitis B infection, where hepatocytes display a granular, homogenous eosinophilic cytoplasm due to the accumulation of HBsAg in the swollen smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

 

 

Councilman bodies (Option C):

Councilman bodies (or acidophilic bodies) are eosinophilic, round structures representing hepatocyte apoptosis. They are typically seen in acute viral hepatitis and indicate severe hepatocellular injury.

 

 

Glycogenated hepatocytes (Option D):

  • Glycogenated hepatocytes are hepatocytes with increased intracytoplasmic glycogen content.
  • This finding is often seen in conditions associated with metabolic disturbances, such as glycogen storage diseases or acute fatty liver of pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old female infant presents with feeding difficulties and a noticeable facial deformity. On examination, the infant has a unilateral complete cleft involving the left lip, extending through the alveolus and hard palate, with an intact soft palate on the left side. The right side of the lip and palate are completely intact. What is the LAHSAL classification for this patient's cleft abnormality?
questions.stemHtml: A 3-month-old female infant presents with feeding difficulties and a noticeable facial deformity. On examination, the infant has a unilateral complete cleft involving the left lip, extending through the alveolus and hard palate, with an intact soft palate on the left side. The right side of the lip and palate are completely intact. What is the LAHSAL classification for this patient's cleft abnormality?
questions.solution: nderstanding LAHSAL Classification: LAHSAL is a system used to describe cleft lip and palate in a topographic and symmetrical manner, from the patient's right to left : Letter Meaning L Lip A Alveolus H Hard palate S Soft palate Capital letter Complete cleft Lowercase letter Incomplete cleft "0" Normal segment So: The first 3 letters (L-A-H) refer to the right side The last 3 letters (S-A-L) refer to the left side Breakdown of the Case: Left side : Lip cleft → L (complete, hence capital) Alveolus cleft → A Hard palate cleft → H Soft palate is intact → S = 0 Right side : Everything intact → L-A-H = 0-0-0 Putting this into LAHSAL: Right side (L-A-H) = 0-0-0 Left side (S-A-L) = H-A-L (from back to front) Final Code (Right to Left) = 00HSAL LAH000 (Option B): Incorrect, implies cleft on right side. LAHS00 (Option C): Incorrect, implies soft palate cleft on right and lip/alveolus normal. LAHSAL (Option D): Implies bilateral complete cleft (both sides involved). @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
nderstanding LAHSAL Classification:

LAHSAL is a system used to describe cleft lip and palate in a topographic and symmetrical manner, from the patient's right to left:

Letter Meaning
L Lip
A Alveolus
H Hard palate
S Soft palate
Capital letter Complete cleft
Lowercase letter Incomplete cleft
"0" Normal segment

 

So:

  • The first 3 letters (L-A-H) refer to the right side

  • The last 3 letters (S-A-L) refer to the left side

Breakdown of the Case:

  • Left side:

    • Lip cleft → L (complete, hence capital)

    • Alveolus cleft → A

    • Hard palate cleft → H

    • Soft palate is intact → S = 0

  • Right side: Everything intact → L-A-H = 0-0-0

Putting this into LAHSAL:

  • Right side (L-A-H) = 0-0-0

  • Left side (S-A-L) = H-A-L (from back to front)

Final Code (Right to Left) = 00HSAL

 

LAH000 (Option B): Incorrect, implies cleft on right side.

LAHS00 (Option C): Incorrect, implies soft palate cleft on right and lip/alveolus normal.

LAHSAL (Option D): Implies bilateral complete cleft (both sides involved).

DeLancey Level of Support

Ligaments Involved

Conditions

Level 1
  • Supported by uterosacral and cardinal ligaments
  • Supports the uterus and vaginal vault.
  • The cervix remains at or just above the ischial spines.

Damage can lead to:

  • Uterine descent
  • Enterocele
  • Vault descent

Level 2
  • Supported by pelvic fascia and paracolpos, the vagina connects to the lateral pelvic wall via the arcus tendinous fascia pelvis.
  • Includes pubocervical fascia (anteriorly), rectovaginal fascia, and septum (posteriorly).

Damage can lead to:

  • Cystocele
  • Rectocele

Level 3
  • Supported by the levator ani muscle.
  • Supports the lower one-third of the vagina.
  • Forms a platform that compresses pelvic organs (uterus and upper vagina) during straining.

Damage can lead to:

  • Urethrocele
  • Gaping introitus 
  • Deficient perineum

questions.stem: The following sign in breast MRI is characteristic of:
questions.stemHtml: The following sign in breast MRI is characteristic of:
questions.solution: The "Linguine Sign" is a characteristic MRI finding of an intracapsular breast implant rupture . Intracapsular Rupture : The implant shell breaks, but the fibrous capsule remains intact, preventing silicone from leaking out. On MRI, the collapsed shell appears as multiple wavy lines, resembling linguine. On USG, it appears a stepladder appearance. Extracapsular Rupture : Silicone escapes beyond the fibrous capsule, often seen as the "Snowstorm Sign" on ultrasound. (Option C) Other MRI Signs: "Keyhole Sign" / "Teardrop Sign" : Silicone on both sides of a radial fold suggests rupture. "Salad Oil Sign" : Seen in double-lumen implant rupture with mixing of saline and silicone. Management: Surgical removal is recommended to prevent silicone migration and complications. Fibrocystic breast disease (Option A) : Benign condition with lumpy, painful breasts. Common imaging findings include cystic changes, fibrosis, and adenosis . Fat necrosis of the breast (Option D) : Occurs due to trauma or surgery, presenting as oil cysts, calcifications, or irregular masses on mammography or ultrasound. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The "Linguine Sign" is a characteristic MRI finding of an intracapsular breast implant rupture.

  • Intracapsular Rupture: The implant shell breaks, but the fibrous capsule remains intact, preventing silicone from leaking out.
    • On MRI, the collapsed shell appears as multiple wavy lines, resembling linguine.
    • On USG, it appears a stepladder appearance.
  • Extracapsular Rupture: Silicone escapes beyond the fibrous capsule, often seen as the "Snowstorm Sign" on ultrasound. (Option C)

Other MRI Signs:

  • "Keyhole Sign" / "Teardrop Sign": Silicone on both sides of a radial fold suggests rupture.
  • "Salad Oil Sign": Seen in double-lumen implant rupture with mixing of saline and silicone.

Management: Surgical removal is recommended to prevent silicone migration and complications.

 

Fibrocystic breast disease (Option A):

  • Benign condition with lumpy, painful breasts. Common imaging findings include cystic changes, fibrosis, and adenosis.

 

Fat necrosis of the breast (Option D):

  • Occurs due to trauma or surgery, presenting as oil cysts, calcifications, or irregular masses on mammography or ultrasound.

questions.solution: p; Exon : An exon is a coding region of a gene that contains the genetic information necessary for producing a functional protein. Intron : An intron is a non-coding region of a gene that intervenes between exons. During gene expression, introns are removed from the pre-mRNA molecule through splicing, which allows exons to be joined together to form the final mRNA transcript before translation into a protein. Locus : A locus refers to the specific location of a gene or DNA sequence on a chromosome. Allele : An allele is one of the alternate forms of a single gene occupying a given position in a chromosome , which can lead to different traits or characteristics. Alleles can be dominant or recessive. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with severe hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, growth retardation, irritability, and lethargy between feedings. Laboratory tests reveal elevated lactate, triglycerides, and uric acid. The child frequently feeds to manage hypoglycemia. Based on these findings, which condition is most likely responsible for the symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 6-month-old infant presents with severe hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, growth retardation, irritability, and lethargy between feedings. Laboratory tests reveal elevated lactate, triglycerides, and uric acid. The child frequently feeds to manage hypoglycemia. Based on these findings, which condition is most likely responsible for the symptoms?
questions.solution: Von Gierke's Disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I) is caused by a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase , impairing glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis. The key clinical features in this infant, such as severe hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, growth retardation, irritability, and lethargy between feedings , strongly suggest impaired glucose release from the liver. Laboratory findings of elevated lactate, triglycerides, and uric acid further support Von Gierke’s disease due to defective glucose metabolism. Frequent feedings are characteristic, as affected infants need continuous glucose intake to prevent hypoglycemia. Von Gierke's Disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I) Cause Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase enzyme Pathophysiology Inability to convert glucose-6-phosphate to glucose; leads to accumulation of glycogen, lactate, and triglycerides Symptoms Severe hypoglycemia Hepatomegaly and Renomegaly Growth retardation Lactic acidosis Hyperuricemia and Hyperlipidemia Diagnosis Biochemical tests (hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia) Genetic testing Management Frequent feedings with slow-release carbohydrates Blood glucose monitoring Medications for associated conditions Liver transplantation (in severe cases) Glycogen Storage Disorders (GSDs) GSD Type Name Enzyme Deficiency Affected Organs Key Features Type I Von Gierke's Disease Glucose-6-phosphatase Liver, Kidney Severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia Type V McArdle's Disease (Option B ruled out) Muscle phosphorylase Skeletal Muscle Exercise intolerance, muscle cramps, myoglobinuria after exertion Type VII Tarui's Disease (Option C ruled out) Muscle phosphofructokinase Muscle, RBCs Exercise intolerance, muscle cramps, hemolytic anemia Type VI Hers' Disease (Option D ruled out) Liver phosphorylase Liver Hepatomegaly, mild hypoglycemia, milder symptoms than Von Gierke's McArdle's Disease (Option B): Incorrect because it primarily affects muscle , leading to exercise intolerance and myoglobinuria rather than hypoglycemia. Tarui's Disease (Option C): Incorrect because it affects muscle and red blood cells , leading to exercise intolerance and hemolytic anemia , not hypoglycemia. Hers' Disease (Option D): Incorrect because it causes mild hypoglycemia without lactic acidosis , whereas this case presents with severe hypoglycemia and metabolic abnormalities . @Neet_pg_bot

Cause

Management

Lab investigations reveal prolonged bleeding time, prolonged aPTT, and a normal PT. A detailed history and a pedigree analysis were obtained, suspecting a genetic disorder. Based on the pedigree chart, what is this condition's most likely inheritance pattern?
questions.solution: p>The clinical presentation of a female with frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, prolonged bleeding time & aPTT, and normal PT is suggestive of Von Willebrand disease. Platelet Function & Factor VIII – 1-Molybdenum Deficiency Platelet Adhesion: Factor VIII is part of the intrinsic coagulation pathway 1-Molybdenum deficiency → defective platelet adhesion → bleeding time ↑ Coagulation Defect: Factor VIII cannot function normally → factor VIII activity ↓ Leads to prolonged APTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) The pedigree chart shows a vertical transmission pattern with no skipping of generations and is suggestive of autosomal dominant inheritance. Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern: The mode of transmission is vertical . An affected person has an affected parent. There is a 50% chance of the dominant trait being transmitted to offspring. Both males and females are equally affected. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
p>The clinical presentation of a female with frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, prolonged bleeding time & aPTT, and normal PT is suggestive of Von Willebrand disease.

 

Platelet Function & Factor VIII – 1-Molybdenum Deficiency

  • Platelet Adhesion:

    • Factor VIII is part of the intrinsic coagulation pathway

    • 1-Molybdenum deficiency → defective platelet adhesion → bleeding time ↑

  • Coagulation Defect:

    • Factor VIII cannot function normally → factor VIII activity ↓

    • Leads to prolonged APTT (activated partial thromboplastin time)

The pedigree chart shows a vertical transmission pattern with no skipping of generations and is suggestive of autosomal dominant inheritance.

Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern:

  • The mode of transmission is vertical. An affected person has an affected parent.
  • There is a 50% chance of the dominant trait being transmitted to offspring.
  • Both males and females are equally affected.

questions.stem: A forensic pathologist is examining the lungs of a newborn during an autopsy. The lungs appear mottled in color and occupy most of the thoracic cavity. However, when subjected to the hydrostatic test, portions of the lung tissue sink while others float. Microscopically, some areas show expanded alveoli lined with flat squamous cells, while other areas show closed alveoli lined with cuboidal cells. What is the most likely explanation for these conflicting findings?
questions.stemHtml: A forensic pathologist is examining the lungs of a newborn during an autopsy. The lungs appear mottled in color and occupy most of the thoracic cavity. However, when subjected to the hydrostatic test, portions of the lung tissue sink while others float. Microscopically, some areas show expanded alveoli lined with flat squamous cells, while other areas show closed alveoli lined with cuboidal cells. What is the most likely explanation for these conflicting findings?

options.label: A
options.text: The infant was stillborn, and the floating lung portions are due to putrefaction

options.label: B
options.text: The infant was live-born but suffered from severe respiratory distress syndrome

options.label: C
options.text: The infant was live-born and partially breathed before death

options.label: D
options.text: The findings are inconclusive and could be due to artificial respiration attempts

questions.answerText: The infant was live-born and partially breathed before death
questions.solution: expansion, indicating some aeration. Mixed hydrostatic test results- some lung parts floated while others sank. Microscopy showed: Expanded alveoli lined with flat squamous cells (indicating respiration). Closed alveoli lined with cuboidal/columnar cells (indicating unrespired areas). Comparison: Respired vs. Unrespired Lung Feature Unrespired Lung (Stillborn) Respired Lung (Live-born) Color Bluish red Mottled Volume Small Large, covers heart Thoracic cavity Not full Fully occupied Pleura Loose, wrinkled Taut, stretched Margins Sharp Rounded Surface Smooth Uneven Consistency Dense, firm, non-crepitant (liver-like) Soft, spongy, elastic, crepitant Ploucquet's test 1:70 1:35 Fodere's static test 30–40 g 60–70 g Diaphragm level 4th–5th rib 6th–7th rib Blood oozing Little, frothless Abundant, frothy Hydrostatic test Whole and parts sink in water Floats in water Alveoli Not expanded Expanded Microscopy Closed sacs with cuboidal/columnar lining Dilated sacs with flat squamous lining and vascularity The infant was stillborn, and the floating lung portions are due to putrefaction (Option A): Incorrect because although putrefaction can produce gas leading to lung flotation, microscopy revealed expanded alveoli with flattened squamous cells , indicating actual respiration, not decomposition. The infant was live-born but suffered from severe respiratory distress syndrome (Option B): Incorrect because RDS usually leads to generalized alveolar collapse , not the mixed pattern of both inflated and collapsed alveoli observed here. The findings are inconclusive and could be due to artificial respiration attempt (Option D): Incorrect because artificial respiration typically causes more uniform aeration of the lungs . The patchy aeration pattern and histological evidence of both respired and unrespired areas support partial natural breathing , not artificial intervention alone. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman reports that for the past year, she has been experiencing severe anxiety whenever she leaves her home alone and while using public transport. She fears that if she experiences dizziness or shortness of breath, she will not be able to find help. Due to this fear, she has been unable to visit friends, shop, or attend social events without a companion. She has never had a panic attack. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman reports that for the past year, she has been experiencing severe anxiety whenever she leaves her home alone and while using public transport. She fears that if she experiences dizziness or shortness of breath, she will not be able to find help. Due to this fear, she has been unable to visit friends, shop, or attend social events without a companion. She has never had a panic attack. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: This patient’s symptoms are classic for agoraphobia , a condition defined by marked fear or anxiety about being in situations where escape might be difficult or help might not be available in the event of developing panic-like or incapacitating symptoms (e.g., dizziness, shortness of breath). Key features from the case: Fear of leaving home alone Avoidance of public settings (e.g., shopping, visiting friends, attending events) Requires a companion to feel safe No history of panic attacks (which rules out panic disorder) Agoraphobia can occur with or without panic disorder . In this case, her fear is anticipatory (fear of what might happen), not a response to actual panic attacks. Agoraphobia – Diagnostic Criteria Highlights (DSM-5): Criterion Description Fear/anxiety about ≥2 situations e.g., using public transport, open spaces, enclosed places, standing in line or being in a crowd, being outside the home alone Thoughts Escape might be difficult or help unavailable Behavior Actively avoided or endured with intense fear or only with a companion Duration Typically ≥6 months Not better explained by another condition e.g., social anxiety or specific phobia Treatment: Pharmacological, psychological, and combined treatments. Psychological therapies: Behavioral therapy: For rapid and complete reduction of agoraphobia, such as systematic desensitization, graded exposure. Cognitive Behavioral therapy Virtual therapy Relaxation techniques Pharmacotherapy: Limited role. Used to treat comorbid conditions like panic disorder. SSRIs, along with Benzodiazepines (short-term). Panic Disorder (Option A): Characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks and persistent concern about having future attacks lasting more than a month. Patients often develop anticipatory anxiety and behavioral changes, such as avoiding places where attacks have previously occurred. In this case, the primary concern is about avoiding situations due to fear of panic attacks, not recurrent panic attacks themselves. This option is incorrect. Specific Phobia (Option B): Specific phobia refers to an intense fear of a particular object or situation (e.g., heights, animals, flying). The avoidance behavior in this case is not related to a specific object but to broader situations where escape might be difficult, which is more characteristic of agoraphobia. This option is incorrect. Social anxiety disorder (Option C): It involves an intense fear of being judged or embarrassed in social or performance situations. The avoidance behavior in this case is not driven by fear of social scrutiny but by fear of being in places where escape might be difficult in case of a panic-like situation. This option is incorrect. @Neet_pg_bot

The surgeon needs to perform anastomosis to reconstruct the digestive tract after removing the affected tissues. In which sequence are the anastomoses typically performed during a Whipple procedure?
questions.stemHtml: A patient is scheduled to undergo a Whipple procedure for the treatment of pancreatic cancer. The surgeon needs to perform anastomosis to reconstruct the digestive tract after removing the affected tissues. In which sequence are the anastomoses typically performed during a Whipple procedure?
questions.solution: data-dictid="7fb96d08421692777181e532c3c653">anastomosis in a Whipple procedure is to start with the pancreaticojejunostomy, followed by the hepaticojejunostomy, and finally the gastrojejunostomy. This order allows for proper reconstruction of the digestive system following the removal of the affected tissues. Whipple’s procedure (Pancreaticoduodenectomy) Structures removed: Head of the pancreas, the first part of the small intestine (duodenum), the gallbladder, and a portion of the bile duct. Types: Pylorus-Preserving Whipple Procedure (Preferred) Non–Pylorus-Preserving Whipple Procedure Indications Pancreatic Cancer: Commonly treated with Whipple if cancer is localized to the head of the pancreas. Chronic Pancreatitis: when uncontrolled by medical management. Tumors in Pancreas/Surrounding Areas: Includes duodenum, distal bile duct, and ampulla of Vater. Procedure Steps Tumor Assessment: Explore abdomen to assess tumor size, location, and spread. Resection: Remove head of pancreas, duodenum, gallbladder, and part of bile duct; this may include partial stomach resection. Lymph Node Dissection: Remove and examine nearby lymph nodes. Reconstruction Pancreaticojejunostomy: Connect remaining pancreas to jejunum. Hepaticojejunostomy: Connect common bile duct to jejunum. Gastrojejunostomy: Connect stomach to jejunum. Anastomosis Principles Tension-Free Connection: Achieve mucosa-to-mucosa connection for healing. Order of Anastomoses: Pancreaticojejunostomy → Hepaticojejunostomy → Gastrojejunostomy Stent Placement: May use internal/external stents for small ducts. Complications Pancreatic Fistula: Major issue; managed with somatostatin analogues. Delayed Gastric Emptying Bleeding, wound infection Reoperation, increased mortality Dumping/Bile Reflux: Common after non-pylorus-preserving Whipple; pylorus-preserving method has uncertain benefits. @Neet_pg_bot

data-dictid="7fb96d08421692777181e532c3c653">anastomosis in a Whipple procedure is to start with the pancreaticojejunostomy, followed by the hepaticojejunostomy, and finally the gastrojejunostomy. This order allows for proper reconstruction of the digestive system following the removal of the affected tissues.

Whipple’s procedure  (Pancreaticoduodenectomy)

Structures removed: Head of the pancreas, the first part of the small intestine (duodenum), the gallbladder, and a portion of the bile duct.

Types:

  • Pylorus-Preserving Whipple Procedure (Preferred)
  • Non–Pylorus-Preserving Whipple Procedure

Indications
  • Pancreatic Cancer: Commonly treated with Whipple if cancer is localized to the head of the pancreas.
  • Chronic Pancreatitis: when uncontrolled by medical management.
  • Tumors in Pancreas/Surrounding Areas: Includes duodenum, distal bile duct, and ampulla of Vater.

Procedure Steps
  • Tumor Assessment: Explore abdomen to assess tumor size, location, and spread.
  • Resection: Remove head of pancreas, duodenum, gallbladder, and part of bile duct; this may include partial stomach resection.
  • Lymph Node Dissection: Remove and examine nearby lymph nodes.

Reconstruction
  • Pancreaticojejunostomy: Connect remaining pancreas to jejunum.
  • Hepaticojejunostomy: Connect common bile duct to jejunum.
  • Gastrojejunostomy: Connect stomach to jejunum.

Anastomosis Principles
  • Tension-Free Connection: Achieve mucosa-to-mucosa connection for healing.
  • Order of Anastomoses: Pancreaticojejunostomy → Hepaticojejunostomy → Gastrojejunostomy
  • Stent Placement: May use internal/external stents for small ducts.

Complications
  • Pancreatic Fistula: Major issue; managed with somatostatin analogues.
  • Delayed Gastric Emptying
  • Bleeding, wound infection
  • Reoperation, increased mortality
  • Dumping/Bile Reflux: Common after non-pylorus-preserving Whipple; pylorus-preserving method has uncertain benefits.

an class="customMeta" data-dictid="db46007ad21692777192dcc160a2e2">medial deviation of the right ureter. A retro-caval ureter is caused by a developmental anomaly in which the ureter is trapped behind the IVC due to improper embryological development of the vena cava. This leads to a characteristic medial deviation of the ureter at the L3-L4 level. Patients with this condition often present with flank pain, recurrent urinary tract infections, and hydronephrosis due to impaired urine flow through the kinked or obstructed ureter. 

 

 

 

Vesicoureteral reflux (Option A): This condition occurs when urine flows backwards from the bladder into the ureters, leading to recurrent urinary infections and kidney damage. While it can result in hydronephrosis and recurrent infections, it is not associated with medial deviation of the ureter.

 

Transitional cell carcinoma (Option B): This type of cancer affects the lining of the urinary tract, most commonly the bladder and ureters. It can cause symptoms like hematuria and flank pain, but it is not associated with the specific imaging feature of medial deviation of the ureter. Instead, transitional cell carcinoma typically presents with filling defects and dilatation of the ureter above the tumour giving a, known as the "goblet sign," and does not lead to the ureter passing behind the IVC. 

 

 

Polycystic kidney disease (Option C): This genetic disorder is characterised by the growth of numerous fluid-filled cysts in the kidneys, leading to enlarged kidneys and impaired function and is not linked to ureter deviation or hydronephrosis.

questions.solution: dy> Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome Definition Rare X-linked recessive disorder affecting males; characterized by eczema, thrombocytopenia, and immunodeficiency. Genetic Basis Caused by mutations in the WASP gene, affecting actin cytoskeleton in blood cells. Clinical Features Eczema : Develops within the first year; ranges from mild to severe. Thrombocytopenia: Present at birth; leads to prolonged bleeding from the umbilical stump , easy bruising, petechiae , and purpura. Mnemonic: WATER - WA SP gene mutation, T hrombocytopenia, E czema, R ecurrent infections Treatment Supportive Care: Preventative antibiotics, immunoglobulin replacement, eczema management, use of killed vaccines. Curative Treatment: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) Prognosis Without HSCT: Often fatal in childhood due to infections, bleeding, or malignancies. Henoch-Schonlein purpura (Option B) is characterised by palpable purpura, joint Involvement, abdominal pain, and renal involvement, but does not usually present with eczema or thrombocytopenia. questions.solutionHtml:
dy>

Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome

Definition

  • Rare X-linked recessive disorder affecting males; characterized by eczema, thrombocytopenia, and immunodeficiency.

Genetic Basis

  • Caused by mutations in the WASP gene, affecting actin cytoskeleton in blood cells.

Clinical Features

  • Eczema: Develops within the first year; ranges from mild to severe.
  • Thrombocytopenia: Present at birth; leads to prolonged bleeding from the umbilical stump, easy bruising, petechiae, and purpura.
  • Immunodeficiency: Susceptible to infections (bacterial, viral, opportunistic); increased risk of autoimmune disorders and malignancies (lymphomas, leukemia).

Diagnosis

  • Clinical Triad: Eczema, thrombocytopenia, and immunodeficiency.
  • Lab Tests: CBC (small, abnormally shaped platelets), immunoglobulin levels (low IgM, high IgA and IgE), lymphocyte subset analysis (low T cells), genetic testing (WASP mutations).
  • Mnemonic: WATER-WASP gene mutation, Thrombocytopenia, Eczema, Recurrent infections

Treatment

  • Supportive Care: Preventative antibiotics, immunoglobulin replacement, eczema management, use of killed vaccines.
  • Curative Treatment: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)

Prognosis

  • Without HSCT: Often fatal in childhood due to infections, bleeding, or malignancies.
  • With HSCT: Can significantly improve life expectancy; risks include graft-versus-host disease (GvHD).

 

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) (Option A) presents with severe immunodeficiency but typically lacks thrombocytopenia or small platelets.

 

Henoch-Schonlein purpura (Option B) is characterised by palpable purpura, joint Involvement, abdominal pain, and renal involvement, but does not usually present with eczema or thrombocytopenia.

 

Ataxia-Telangiectasia (Option D) involves cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasia and immunodeficiency but does not present with thrombocytopenia or eczema.

ae4">Temporal association

Explanation:

The given scenario is an example of Temporal association.

Temporal association:

  • The cause must precede the observed effect.
  • In chronic diseases, establishing temporal sequence can be challenging due to insidious onset and ignorance of precise induction periods.
  • Example: Lung cancer occurring in long-term smokers satisfies the temporal requirement.

 

Hill's criteria for causation are a group of 9 principles that can be useful in establishing epidemiologic evidence of a causal relationship between a presumed cause and an observed effect and have been widely used in public health research.

Different principles are as follows:

  • Temporality
  • Strength
  • Specificity
  • Consistency
  • Plausibility
  • Coherence
  • Analogy
  • Gradient
  • Experiment

 

Strength of association (Option B) refers to how strong the link is between exposure and disease (e.g., measured statistically with risk ratios).

Consistency of association(Option C) refers to whether the same association is observed across different studies and populations

Biological plausibility(Option D) refers to whether the association makes sense based on known biological mechanisms (asbestos causing mesothelioma is biologically plausible, but that's not what's being illustrated here).

questions.stem: Identify the diagnosis related to the image:
questions.stemHtml: Identify the diagnosis related to the image:
questions.solution: a typical presentation of Twin Reversed Arterial Perfusion (TRAP) Sequence , characterized by an acardiac twin, an amorphous mass without a heart, and a normal twin. The acardiac twin receives blood from the normal twin via A-V anastomosis , which can lead to high-output cardiac failure in the normal twin. This deoxygenated blood, which keeps the recipient twin alive, however, goes only to the baby's lower limb, resulting in a mass of flesh with a very small head and properly formed lower limbs . There’s also an impending risk of cardiac failure in the donor baby as it is pumping blood to itself as well as into the recipient baby. Diagnosis is mainly done by USG Doppler or MRI . The main modality of treatment is by ligation of the umbilical cord (laser or RFA) of the acardiac twin under fetoscopic guidance. @Neet_pg_bot

Audiometry shows hearing loss predominantly in lower frequencies, and otoscopic examination reveals a normal tympanic membrane. The patient denies experiencing tinnitus or vertigo. The patient’s hearing loss is mild and not significantly affecting his daily life. What is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male presents with progressive hearing loss in his left ear over the past few years. Audiometry shows hearing loss predominantly in lower frequencies, and otoscopic examination reveals a normal tympanic membrane. The patient denies experiencing tinnitus or vertigo. The patient’s hearing loss is mild and not significantly affecting his daily life. What is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this patient?
questions.solution: p> In mild cases of stapedial otosclerosis where hearing loss is not significantly impacting daily life, observation with regular hearing tests is the preferred initial approach. Medical Management of Otosclerosis Management is individualized based on whether the otosclerosis is stapedial (middle ear) or cochlear (inner ear), focusing on hearing loss and quality of life. For Stapedial Otosclerosis Observation & Monitoring: (Option C) Recommended for mild cases or when hearing loss is not severe. Regular audiograms track hearing loss progression. Hearing Aids: Effective for conductive hearing loss due to the fixed stapes. Non-invasive option to improve sound transmission. For Cochlear Otosclerosis Hearing Aids: May help but are less effective for severe sensorineural hearing loss. Symptom Management: Tinnitus: Managed with sound or tinnitus retraining therapy. Vertigo: May improve with hearing treatment; other therapies could be needed. Medications for otosclerosis: Treatment Mechanism Duration Benefits Sodium Fluoride (NaF) (Option D) Stabilizes hearing thresholds and vestibular symptoms. Combined with calcium carbonate and vitamin D for enhanced effect. At least 6 months Delays worsening tinnitus Reduces conductive and sensorineural hearing loss Bisphosphonates (Option B) Stabilizes hearing loss, reduces dizziness and tinnitus. At least 6 months Stabilizes hearing loss Relieves vestibular symptoms Immediate stapedectomy surgery (Option A) : Surgery is considered in more advanced or symptomatic cases. In case of bilateral otosclerosis the worse ear is operated first and a wait time of 6 months is warranted before next surgery. C/I: Positive Schwartz sign, Pregnancy, active infection, only hearing ear, flying, diving and working at height. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
p>

In mild cases of stapedial otosclerosis where hearing loss is not significantly impacting daily life, observation with regular hearing tests is the preferred initial approach.

 

Medical Management of Otosclerosis

Management is individualized based on whether the otosclerosis is stapedial (middle ear) or cochlear (inner ear), focusing on hearing loss and quality of life.

 

For Stapedial Otosclerosis

  • Observation & Monitoring: (Option C)
    • Recommended for mild cases or when hearing loss is not severe.
    • Regular audiograms track hearing loss progression.
  • Hearing Aids:
    • Effective for conductive hearing loss due to the fixed stapes.
    • Non-invasive option to improve sound transmission.

 

For Cochlear Otosclerosis

  • Hearing Aids:
    • May help but are less effective for severe sensorineural hearing loss.
  • Symptom Management:
    • Tinnitus: Managed with sound or tinnitus retraining therapy.
    • Vertigo: May improve with hearing treatment; other therapies could be needed.

 

Medications for otosclerosis:

Treatment

Mechanism

Duration

Benefits

Sodium Fluoride (NaF) (Option D)

Stabilizes hearing thresholds and vestibular symptoms. Combined with calcium carbonate and vitamin D for enhanced effect.

At least 6 months

Delays worsening tinnitus

Reduces conductive and sensorineural hearing loss

Bisphosphonates (Option B)

Stabilizes hearing loss, reduces dizziness and tinnitus.

At least 6 months

Stabilizes hearing loss

Relieves vestibular symptoms

 

Immediate stapedectomy surgery (Option A): Surgery is considered in more advanced or symptomatic cases. In case of bilateral otosclerosis the worse ear is operated first and a wait time of 6 months is warranted before next surgery. C/I: Positive Schwartz sign, Pregnancy, active infection, only hearing ear, flying, diving and working at height.

questions.stem: An ultrasound image of the gallbladder is consistent with a congenital anatomical variant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: An ultrasound image of the gallbladder is consistent with a congenital anatomical variant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: d16927771840c9e29f164">congenital variant of the gallbladder characterized by a fold at the fundus that resembles a cap. It is a benign condition and is typically asymptomatic, with its appearance being consistent with a cap-like structure on ultrasound. It has no pathological significance and does not affect gallbladder function. A floating gallbladder (or gallbladder volvulus) (Option A) refers to abnormal positioning of the gallbladder within the abdominal cavity, often due to the presence of an abnormally long mesentery from the gallbladder to the liver bed, allowing it to float freely. This makes the gallbladder prone to volvulus. This condition does not present as a cap-like fold on ultrasound. An accessory gallbladder (Option B) is a rare condition where an additional gallbladder exists alongside the normal one. It appears as a separate entity on imaging. A gallbladder septum (Option D) is an abnormal partition within the gallbladder that can be mistaken for a Phrygian cap. It appears as a distinct partition. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 6 y/o child weighs 20 kg and requires maintenance fluid based on the Holliday-Segar formula. What is the correct amount of fluid the child should receive in 24 hours?
questions.solution: Explanation: Using the Holliday-Segar "4-2-1" rule : To calculate maintenance fluid per hour: First 10kgs × 4= a Next 10kgs × 2= b Next kgs × 1= c Total = a+b+c Hence, for this patient: For the first 10 kg of weight: 4 mL/kg/hour → 4 mL × 10 kg = 40 mL/hour For the next 10 kg (10-20 kg): 2 mL/kg/hour → 2 mL × 10 kg = 20 mL/hour Total per hour: 40 mL + 20 mL = 60 mL/hour In 24 hours: 60 mL/hour × 24 hours = 1440 mL (rounded to 1500 mL ) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

To calculate maintenance fluid per hour:

  • First 10kgs × 4= a
  • Next 10kgs × 2= b
  • Next kgs × 1= c
  • Total = a+b+c

 

Hence, for this patient:

  • For the next 10 kg (10-20 kg): 2 mL/kg/hour → 2 mL × 10 kg = 20 mL/hour

questions.stem: A 57-year-old male smoker with a persistent cough and weight loss is found to have a lung mass on imaging. The biopsy showed keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. Which of the following paraneoplastic syndromes is highly associated with this diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 57-year-old male smoker with a persistent cough and weight loss is found to have a lung mass on imaging. The biopsy showed keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. Which of the following paraneoplastic syndromes is highly associated with this diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH)

questions.solution: Explanation: The given clinical presentation and histological findings point towards the diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma, one of the major subtypes of non-small cell lung cancer, which typically arises from the central bronchi and can cause symptoms like coughing, chest pain, and hemoptysis. Hypercalcemia is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. SCC of the lung can produce parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) , leading to elevated calcium levels in the blood. This condition is characterised by symptoms such as fatigue, confusion, excessive thirst and urination, and nausea. Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH) (Option B): It is more commonly associated with small cell lung cancer rather than SCC. SIADH leads to excessive release of antidiuretic hormone, causing water retention and dilutional hyponatremia, which can result in symptoms like muscle cramps, nausea, headaches, and disorientation. Migratory thrombophlebitis (also known as Trousseau’s syndrome) (Option C): While this can be seen in many types of cancers, it is typically more associated with adenocarcinoma rather than with SCC. This syndrome involves the formation of blood clots that migrate within the venous system. Cushing's syndrome (Option D): It is characterised by the ectopic production of ACTH, most frequently associated with small cell lung cancer, not SCC. Patients may experience symptoms such as weight gain, muscle weakness, and a rounded face (moon face). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male presents with hoarseness of voice and breathing difficulties following minor neck trauma. During evaluation, imaging reveals calcified structures in the laryngeal region. What is the most likely cause for this finding?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male presents with hoarseness of voice and breathing difficulties following minor neck trauma. During evaluation, imaging reveals calcified structures in the laryngeal region. What is the most likely cause for this finding?

options.label: A
options.text: Displacement of the thyroid cartilage from its normal position

options.label: B
options.text: Formation of fibrous tissue in the cricoid cartilage

options.label: C
options.text: Inflammatory changes in the arytenoid cartilage

questions.solution: p> Explanation: The cricoid cartilage, made of hyaline cartilage , tends to calcify as part of the aging process, typically beginning around 25 and completing by 65, leading to changes seen on imaging. Cricoid Cartilage Complete ring : The only laryngeal cartilage forms a full ring, resembling a signet ring with a broader posterior lamina and a narrow anterior arch. Articulations : Forms the cricothyroid joint with the thyroid cartilage, allowing rotation along a transverse axis. Forms the cricoarytenoid joint with the arytenoid cartilages, permitting rotational and gliding movements, which control vocal cord motion. Attachments : The cricotracheal membrane connects it to the first tracheal ring. The cricovocal membrane attaches to its arch, forming the vocal ligament. Clinical relevance : In children, the cricoid cartilage is smaller in diameter than the glottis, making it the narrowest part of the airway, crucial for choosing the correct endotracheal tube size. Calcification in older adults can appear as a foreign body on X-rays. Subglottic foreign bodies may lodge near the cricoid cartilage, especially in children. Displacement of the thyroid cartilage from its normal position (Option A): Displacement of the thyroid cartilage, such as dislocation from the cricoid, is not suggested by the presence of calcified structures on imaging. Formation of fibrous tissue in the cricoid cartilage (Option B): The cricoid cartilage is primarily hyaline cartilage, and fibrous tissue is not a typical finding.it can be associated with prolonged ET tube insertion Inflammatory changes in the arytenoid cartilage (Option C): Inflammatory conditions of the arytenoid cartilage might cause vocal cord dysfunction or airway obstruction, but would not lead to calcified structures in the cricoid cartilage. @Neet_pg_bot

p> 

Explanation:

The cricoid cartilage, made of hyaline cartilage, tends to calcify as part of the aging process, typically beginning around 25 and completing by 65, leading to changes seen on imaging.

 

Cricoid Cartilage

  • Complete ring: The only laryngeal cartilage forms a full ring, resembling a signet ring with a broader posterior lamina and a narrow anterior arch.
  • Articulations:
    • Forms the cricothyroid joint with the thyroid cartilage, allowing rotation along a transverse axis.
    • Forms the cricoarytenoid joint with the arytenoid cartilages, permitting rotational and gliding movements, which control vocal cord motion.
  • Attachments:
    • The cricotracheal membrane connects it to the first tracheal ring.
    • The cricovocal membrane attaches to its arch, forming the vocal ligament.
  • Clinical relevance:
    • In children, the cricoid cartilage is smaller in diameter than the glottis, making it the narrowest part of the airway, crucial for choosing the correct endotracheal tube size.
    • Calcification in older adults can appear as a foreign body on X-rays.
    • Subglottic foreign bodies may lodge near the cricoid cartilage, especially in children.

Displacement of the thyroid cartilage from its normal position (Option A): Displacement of the thyroid cartilage, such as dislocation from the cricoid, is not suggested by the presence of calcified structures on imaging.

 

Formation of fibrous tissue in the cricoid cartilage (Option B): The cricoid cartilage is primarily hyaline cartilage, and fibrous tissue is not a typical finding.it can be associated with prolonged ET tube insertion

 

Inflammatory changes in the arytenoid cartilage (Option C): Inflammatory conditions of the arytenoid cartilage might cause vocal cord dysfunction or airway obstruction, but would not lead to calcified structures in the cricoid cartilage.

questions.solution: oriasis, often seen in children and adolescents . It typically occurs 1–3 weeks after a streptococcal pharyngitis or upper respiratory tract infection. The appropriate treatment includes: Eradication of the triggering streptococcal infection using penicillin (or amoxicillin) . Topical therapies (like corticosteroids or emollients) may help skin symptoms but do not address the underlying cause. Reassurance may be needed, but antibiotic therapy is essential in acute, post-streptococcal guttate psoriasis. Clinical Features of Guttate Psoriasis: Feature Description Age group Common in children and young adults Trigger Post-streptococcal pharyngitis (esp. Streptococcus pyogenes ) Lesion morphology Multiple, small (<1 cm), erythematous, scaly plaques ("drop-like") Distribution Trunk, proximal limbs Course May resolve spontaneously or evolve into chronic plaque psoriasis Topical corticosteroids (Option A) : Incorrect as first-line monotherapy in acute guttate psoriasis post-infection. Can be used adjunctively , but antibiotic therapy is essential to treat the underlying streptococcal cause. Reassurance (Option B) : Incorrect as sole treatment . Although guttate psoriasis may be self-limited, reassurance alone is not adequate when a recent streptococcal infection is present. questions.stemHtml: Which type of manoeuvre is depicted in the image given below?
questions.solution: urns-Marshall method. The Burns-Marshall method is used in breech presentation to deliver the after-coming head. The baby hangs by its weight while suprapubic pressure is applied downward and backward. Once the nape of the neck is visible under the pubic arch, the baby's ankles are grasped, and steady traction is applied in an upward and forward arc. Simultaneously, the left hand supports the perineum and guides it gently over the face and brow. Malar flexion and shoulder traction (Option B) aims to maintain the baby's head flexion throughout delivery. The left hand supports the malar bones, while the right hand applies traction to the shoulders and suboccipital region. Forceps delivery (Option C) involves using obstetric forceps to grasp and guide the baby's head during delivery. It allows controlled traction directly on the head without transmitting force through the baby's neck. Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit technique (Option D): The obstetrician supports the baby's head with the palm, and the index finger is placed inside the baby's mouth to support the mandible. Traction is applied to the baby's shoulders to guide the head through the birth canal.   • T2: Tumor ≤2 cm, DOI >5 mm and ≤10 mm; or tumor >2 cm but ≤4 cm, and ≤10 mm DOI.
  • T3: Tumor >4 cm; or any tumor >10 mm DOI.
  • T4a: Moderately advanced local disease - Invades through cortical bone, deep/ extrinsic muscle of tongue, maxillary sinus, or skin of the face.
  • T4b: Very advanced local disease - Invades masticator space, pterygoid plates, skull base, or encases internal carotid artery.

N (Regional Lymph Nodes):

  • Nx: Regional lymph nodes cannot be assessed.
  • N0: No regional lymph node metastasis.
  • N1: Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, ≤3 cm in greatest dimension.
  • N2:
    • N2a: Metastasis in a single ipsilateral node, >3 cm but ≤6 cm in greatest dimension.
    • N2b: Metastasis in multiple ipsilateral nodes, all ≤6 cm).
    • N2c: Metastasis in bilateral or contralateral lymph nodes, all ≤6 cm.
  • N3:
    • N3a: Metastasis in a lymph node >6 cm in greatest dimension, ENE(-).
    • N3b: Metastasis in any node(s) with clinically overt ENE(+).

M (Distant Metastasis):

  • M0: No distant metastasis
  • M1: Distant metastasis

T2 N0 M0

T3 N0 M0 or T1-3 N1 M0

Stage IVA

T4a N0-1 M0 or T1-4a N2 M0

Stage IVB

Any T N3 M0 or T4b Any N M0

Stage IVC

Any T Any N M1

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy weighing 18 kg is admitted for minor elective surgery. According to the Holliday-Segar method, what is his estimated daily fluid requirement?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy weighing 18 kg is admitted for minor elective surgery. According to the Holliday-Segar method, what is his estimated daily fluid requirement?
questions.solution: Explanation: The Holliday-Segar method is a widely used approach for calculating maintenance fluid requirements in children. It's based on the child's weight and provides an estimate of daily fluid needs. It estimates a child's energy expenditure in kilocalories and aligns it with their fluid needs. For every 100 kilocalories burned during metabolism, approximately 100 mL of fluid is required to replace the loss. The method assumes that each kilocalorie lost necessitates 1 mL of fluid for adequate replacement. The method uses the following formula: 100 mL/kg for the first 10 kg 50 mL/kg for the next 10 kg (11 - 20 kg) 20 mL/kg for each kg above 20 kg For this 18 kg child: First 10 kg: 10 x 100 mL = 1000 mL Next 8 kg: 8 x 50 mL = 400 mL Total: 1000 + 400 = 1400 mL @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

The Holliday-Segar method is a widely used approach for calculating maintenance fluid requirements in children.

  • It's based on the child's weight and provides an estimate of daily fluid needs.
  • It estimates a child's energy expenditure in kilocalories and aligns it with their fluid needs.
  • For every 100 kilocalories burned during metabolism, approximately 100 mL of fluid is required to replace the loss.
  • The method assumes that each kilocalorie lost necessitates 1 mL of fluid for adequate replacement.

The method uses the following formula:

  • 100 mL/kg for the first 10 kg
  • 50 mL/kg for the next 10 kg (11 - 20 kg)
  • 20 mL/kg for each kg above 20 kg

 

For this 18 kg child:

  • First 10 kg: 10 x 100 mL = 1000 mL
  • Next 8 kg: 8 x 50 mL = 400 mL
  • Total: 1000 + 400 = 1400 mL

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding the contraindications of vaccines?

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.answerText: DPT Vaccine is unsafe in children with Spina bifida
questions.solution: : DPT is safe for children with Spina bifida. DPT is contraindicated in progressive neurological diseases due to its pertussis component, anaphylaxis to the previous dose, and encephalopathy within 7 days of vaccination attributed to no other cause. Post-vaccine fever, inconsolable cry within 48 hours, and seizures within 72 hours of vaccine are relative contraindications of DPT. Spina Bifida is a birth defect where there is incomplete closing of the backbone and membranes around the spinal cord. It is a non-progressive neurological condition. Hence DPT is safe in such patients. All live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy except the yellow fever vaccine (Option A) as the infection's risk outweighs the live vaccine's risk. All Live vaccines are contraindicated in patients on corticosteroids (Option C) since their immune response is suppressed. All vaccines except MMR, measles, rubella & varicella are contraindicated in adults with symptomatic HIV (Option D) whereas none are contraindicated in asymptomatic HIV patients. Contraindications of vaccines: @Neet_pg_bot

DPT is safe for children with Spina bifida.

  • DPT is contraindicated in progressive neurological diseases due to its pertussis component, anaphylaxis to the previous dose, and encephalopathy within 7 days of vaccination attributed to no other cause. 
  • Post-vaccine fever, inconsolable cry within 48 hours, and seizures within 72 hours of vaccine are relative contraindications of DPT.
  • Spina Bifida is a birth defect where there is incomplete closing of the backbone and membranes around the spinal cord. It is a non-progressive neurological condition.
  • Hence DPT is safe in such patients.

All live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy except the yellow fever vaccine (Option A) as the infection's risk outweighs the live vaccine's risk.

All Live vaccines are contraindicated in patients on corticosteroids (Option C) since their immune response is suppressed.

All vaccines except MMR, measles, rubella & varicella are contraindicated in adults with symptomatic HIV (Option D) whereas none are contraindicated in asymptomatic HIV patients.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, living in a malaria-prone area, presents with fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, and recent consumption of fava beans. Lab tests show hemolytic anemia. How does glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency lead to the observed symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, living in a malaria-prone area, presents with fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, and recent consumption of fava beans. Lab tests show hemolytic anemia. How does glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency lead to the observed symptoms?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced NADPH impairs glutathione regeneration, causing hemolytic anemia.

options.label: B
options.text: Increased ribulose-5-phosphate overloads nucleotides, leading to renal failure.

options.label: C
options.text: Impaired glucose-6-phosphate conversion disrupts glycolysis, causing hypoglycemia.

options.label: D
options.text: Decreased ATP production affects muscle function, causing myopathy.

questions.answerText: Reduced NADPH impairs glutathione regeneration, causing hemolytic anemia.
questions.solution: In this patient with G6PD deficiency , the consumption of fava beans triggered oxidative stress . Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is an enzyme involved in the pentose phosphate pathway , which is crucial for producing NADPH . NADPH is necessary to regenerate glutathione , a potent antioxidant that helps protect red blood cells (RBCs) from oxidative damage. In individuals with G6PD deficiency , there is insufficient NADPH production. This makes the RBCs more vulnerable to oxidative stress, such as that caused by fava beans , which contain compounds that can trigger oxidative damage. Without enough NADPH to counteract this stress, RBCs are damaged, leading to hemolysis (destruction of red blood cells). As a result of hemolysis, the patient may experience fatigue , jaundice (due to the release of bilirubin from the breakdown of red blood cells), and dark urine (from the presence of hemoglobin or bilirubin in the urine). Increased ribulose-5-phosphate overloads nucleotides, leading to renal failure (Option B): While ribulose-5-phosphate is a product of the PPP, its accumulation does not directly lead to renal failure. The primary issue in G6PD deficiency is the lack of NADPH and the resulting oxidative damage. Impaired glucose-6-phosphate conversion disrupts glycolysis, causing hypoglycemia (Option C): While G6PD deficiency affects glucose-6-phosphate, it does not significantly disrupt glycolysis to cause hypoglycemia. The primary issue is oxidative stress, not energy deficiency. Decreased ATP production affects muscle function, causing myopathy (Option D): While ATP is important, the PPP is not a major ATP-producing pathway in RBCs. The primary problem is the lack of NADPH and the resulting oxidative damage to the red blood cells. @Neet_pg_bot

• In this patient with G6PD deficiency, the consumption of fava beans triggered oxidative stress. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is an enzyme involved in the pentose phosphate pathway, which is crucial for producing NADPH. NADPH is necessary to regenerate glutathione, a potent antioxidant that helps protect red blood cells (RBCs) from oxidative damage.
  • In individuals with G6PD deficiency, there is insufficient NADPH production. This makes the RBCs more vulnerable to oxidative stress, such as that caused by fava beans, which contain compounds that can trigger oxidative damage. Without enough NADPH to counteract this stress, RBCs are damaged, leading to hemolysis (destruction of red blood cells).
  • As a result of hemolysis, the patient may experience fatigue, jaundice (due to the release of bilirubin from the breakdown of red blood cells), and dark urine (from the presence of hemoglobin or bilirubin in the urine).


Increased ribulose-5-phosphate overloads nucleotides, leading to renal failure (Option B): While ribulose-5-phosphate is a product of the PPP, its accumulation does not directly lead to renal failure. The primary issue in G6PD deficiency is the lack of NADPH and the resulting oxidative damage.

Impaired glucose-6-phosphate conversion disrupts glycolysis, causing hypoglycemia (Option C): While G6PD deficiency affects glucose-6-phosphate, it does not significantly disrupt glycolysis to cause hypoglycemia. The primary issue is oxidative stress, not energy deficiency.

Decreased ATP production affects muscle function, causing myopathy (Option D): While ATP is important, the PPP is not a major ATP-producing pathway in RBCs. The primary problem is the lack of NADPH and the resulting oxidative damage to the red blood cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following best differentiates night-eating syndrome from sleep-related eating disorder?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best differentiates night-eating syndrome from sleep-related eating disorder?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.answerText: Consumption of non-edible foods or substances during eating episodes
questions.solution: Sleep-Related Eating Disorder (SRED) is classified as a parasomnia and involves involuntary eating episodes during sleep , often with impaired awareness or amnesia . A hallmark feature is the consumption of unusual or even non-edible items (e.g., soap, raw meat, cigarettes). Night-Eating Syndrome (NES) is characterized by conscious, delayed eating patterns , including evening hyperphagia and nocturnal awakenings with food intake , but the person is aware and typically does not eat non-food items . Night-Eating Syndrome vs. Sleep-Related Eating Disorder Feature Night-Eating Syndrome (NES) Sleep-Related Eating Disorder (SRED) Awareness during episodes Preserved (fully awake and aware) Absent or impaired (amnesia common) Time of eating Late evening or during night awakenings During sleep, often within parasomnia episodes Control over eating Volitional Involuntary Items consumed Normal food Non-edible or dangerous items often consumed Association with other EDs May coexist with BED or depression May be comorbid with sleep disorders Higher prevalence of comorbid bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder (Option A): Incorrect. While NES may co-occur with BED, this is not the best distinguishing feature compared to SRED. Lack of concern about body image or weight (Option C): Incorrect. Both conditions may present with or without concern about weight, and it’s not a core differentiator. Increased risk of developing obesity and metabolic syndrome (Option D): Incorrect. Both NES and SRED can lead to weight gain and metabolic issues, so this is not unique to either. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Night-Eating Syndrome (NES) is characterized by conscious, delayed eating patterns, including evening hyperphagia and nocturnal awakenings with food intake, but the person is aware and typically does not eat non-food items.

questions.solution: scenario and histopathological findings point towards diagnosing Pilocytic astrocytoma, low-grade brain tumors commonly found in children and young adults. questions.solution: In the case of a 20-year-old woman with metastatic breast carcinoma who is experiencing severe pain (8/10), the best medication to treat her pain would be PO morphine. Morphine is an opioid analgesic that is effective for moderate to severe pain WHO Step Ladder Management of Pain : It is WHO-given criteria for the management of severe chronic pain which is not subsiding even after conventional therapies. Management depends on the severity of pain in a 'ladder ' manner. Step 1 Mild Pain Non-Opioid Analgesics: Acetaminophen, NSAIDs Adjuvant therapies (e.g., corticosteroids,anticonvulsants,antidepressants) Step 2 Moderate Pain Fixed-Dose Combination Products: (e.g., acetaminophen + hydrocodone) Weak Opioids: (e.g., codeine, tramadol) Adjuvant agents as needed Step 3 Severe Pain Strong Opioids: (e.g., morphine, oxycodone) Individualized dosing Appropriate adjuvant therapies Step 4 Complex and Uncontrolled Pain Interventional techniques: (e.g., nerve blocks, neurolysis) Multimodal approaches for complex pain syndromes IV paracetamol (Option A) is less effective for severe pain compared to opioids. questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with vertigo triggered by loud noises. His medical history includes a surgical fenestration for a middle ear condition. Audiometric tests are within normal limits, but vestibular testing reveals abnormal pressure responses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man presents with vertigo triggered by loud noises. His medical history includes a surgical fenestration for a middle ear condition. Audiometric tests are within normal limits, but vestibular testing reveals abnormal pressure responses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Tullio phenomenon is characterised by vertigo, dizziness, or imbalance triggered by loud sounds . This occurs due to an abnormal third window effect in the inner ear, which could be caused by congenital conditions, trauma, or a surgical procedure like fenestration. The pressure changes from sound waves affect the balance organs, particularly the semicircular canals , causing vertigo. Hennebert’s sign (Option A) refers to vertigo or nystagmus induced by pressure changes in the ear without an underlying middle ear infection. It is seen in conditions like syphilis or Meniere’s disease , where pressure on the inner ear (e.g., via the Valsalva manoeuvre) provokes balance disturbances. Lhermitte’s sign (Option C) is an electric shock-like sensation that travels down the spine and into the limbs when the neck is flexed. It is commonly associated with multiple sclerosis or cervical cord compression. Meniere’s disease (Option D) involves episodic vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss, and a sense of fullness in the ear. It results from excess fluid buildup in the inner ear, affecting both hearing and balance. @Neet_pg_bot

• Tullio phenomenon is characterised by vertigo, dizziness, or imbalance triggered by loud sounds.
  • This occurs due to an abnormal third window effect in the inner ear, which could be caused by congenital conditions, trauma, or a surgical procedure like fenestration.
  • The pressure changes from sound waves affect the balance organs, particularly the semicircular canals, causing vertigo.

    • Hennebert’s sign (Option A) refers to vertigo or nystagmus induced by pressure changes in the ear without an underlying middle ear infection. It is seen in conditions like syphilis or Meniere’s disease, where pressure on the inner ear (e.g., via the Valsalva manoeuvre) provokes balance disturbances.

    Lhermitte’s sign (Option C) is an electric shock-like sensation that travels down the spine and into the limbs when the neck is flexed. It is commonly associated with multiple sclerosis or cervical cord compression.

    Meniere’s disease (Option D) involves episodic vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss, and a sense of fullness in the ear. It results from excess fluid buildup in the inner ear, affecting both hearing and balance.
