questions.stem: Which of the following methods of suffocation is most commonly associated with a reflex vagal inhibition that can lead to sudden cardiac arrest?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following methods of suffocation is most commonly associated with a reflex vagal inhibition that can lead to sudden cardiac arrest?
questions.solution: 58371692777185eff2ccabb7">Coronary is a condition characterized by sudden collapse and death while eating, often in intoxicated individuals. The high blood alcohol content anesthetizes the gag reflex, and reflex vagal inhibition can lead to a sudden cardiac arrest. Suffocation Definition : Asphyxia where air entry to the lungs is prevented by means other than pressure on the neck or drowning. Caused by breathing in a vitiated atmosphere (deficient in oxygen). Methods of Suffocation Features Smothering (Option A ruled out) Definition : Closing the nose and mouth using hands or foreign substances (e.g., mud, cloth). Autopsy Findings : External : Pallor may be present around the mouth/nose, pressure marks, distinct nail marks, petechiae, contusion on the inner lip, and stains on the bedding. Internal : Potential internal organ haemorrhages. Gagging (Option B ruled out) Definition : Asphyxia caused by a cloth or material obstructing the mouth and nose. Mechanism : A gag can block the pharynx, initially allowing nasal airflow. Obstruction worsens due to saliva and mucus, leading to complete airway blockage. Symptoms : Facial congestion. Fine petechiae on the face, sclerae, and conjunctivae. Intent : Always homicidal. Choking (Option C ruled out) Definition : Airway obstruction due to an object lodged in the hypopharynx. Accidental Choking : Often occurs during meals, especially while laughing or crying; vomited matter may be inhaled under intoxication or unconsciousness. Immediate Symptoms : Acute respiratory distress; complications may develop later. Autopsy Findings : Thickened epiglottis and folds Mucus accumulation in the throat. Lungs exhibit interalveolar oedema, congestion, and haemorrhages. Café Coronary Definition : Sudden collapse and death while eating, often in intoxicated individuals. Symptoms : Cyanosis and violent coughing. Collapse without significant distress. Cause of Death : Reflex vagal inhibition leading to sudden cardiac arrest; high blood alcohol content anaesthetises the gag reflex. A poorly chewed food bolus may obstruct the larynx. Autopsy Findings : Obstruction may be found in the mouth, larynx, or trachea, with food particles in mucus in the trachea/bronchi, differentiating from cases of post-mortem oesophagal food forcing. Signs of asphyxia may be absent. Treatment: Heimlich Maneuver : Stand behind the patient, interlock fingers, and apply pressure to the stomach. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
58371692777185eff2ccabb7">Coronary is a condition characterized by sudden collapse and death while eating, often in intoxicated individuals.
  • The high blood alcohol content anesthetizes the gag reflex, and reflex vagal inhibition can lead to a sudden cardiac arrest.

Suffocation

  • Definition: Asphyxia where air entry to the lungs is prevented by means other than pressure on the neck or drowning.
  • Caused by breathing in a vitiated atmosphere (deficient in oxygen).

Methods of Suffocation

Features

Smothering

(Option A ruled out)
  • Definition: Closing the nose and mouth using hands or foreign substances (e.g., mud, cloth).
  • Autopsy Findings:
    • External: Pallor may be present around the mouth/nose, pressure marks, distinct nail marks, petechiae, contusion on the inner lip, and stains on the bedding.
    • Internal: Potential internal organ haemorrhages.

Gagging (Option B ruled out)
  • Definition: Asphyxia caused by a cloth or material obstructing the mouth and nose.
  • Mechanism: A gag can block the pharynx, initially allowing nasal airflow. Obstruction worsens due to saliva and mucus, leading to complete airway blockage.
  • Symptoms:
    • Facial congestion.
    • Fine petechiae on the face, sclerae, and conjunctivae.
  • Intent: Always homicidal.

Choking

(Option C ruled out)
  • Definition: Airway obstruction due to an object lodged in the hypopharynx.
  • Accidental Choking: Often occurs during meals, especially while laughing or crying; vomited matter may be inhaled under intoxication or unconsciousness.
  • Immediate Symptoms: Acute respiratory distress; complications may develop later.
  • Autopsy Findings:
    • Thickened epiglottis and folds
    • Mucus accumulation in the throat.
    • Lungs exhibit interalveolar oedema, congestion, and haemorrhages.

Café Coronary
  • Definition: Sudden collapse and death while eating, often in intoxicated individuals.
  • Symptoms:
    • Cyanosis and violent coughing.
    • Collapse without significant distress.
  • Cause of Death: Reflex vagal inhibition leading to sudden cardiac arrest; high blood alcohol content anaesthetises the gag reflex. A poorly chewed food bolus may obstruct the larynx.
  • Autopsy Findings: Obstruction may be found in the mouth, larynx, or trachea, with food particles in mucus in the trachea/bronchi, differentiating from cases of post-mortem oesophagal food forcing. Signs of asphyxia may be absent.

  • Treatment: Heimlich Maneuver: Stand behind the patient, interlock fingers, and apply pressure to the stomach.

questions.solution: immediately discontinued in individuals with elevated serum creatinine levels (>1.5 mg/dL in males and >1.4 mg/dL in females) , as it increases the risk of life-threatening lactic acidosis. Complications associated with Metformin: Renal failure is common with metformin use. Plasma metformin levels are inversely related to GFR due to reduced drug clearance. Current guidelines suggest the safe use of metformin when GFR is more than 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Management: Assess renal function before starting metformin and monitor it annually. Discontinue if serum creatinine >1.5 mg/dL or eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Discontinue pre-emptively before radiographic procedures using contrast dyes (till 48 hours after the procedure until renal function normalises) and hospitalization for severe illness (sepsis). Dose adjustment is needed for cationic drugs excreted by renal tubular secretion, such as cimetidine, furosemide, nifedipine, etc. It is indicated in patients with severe pulmonary disease, heart failure, liver disease, or chronic alcohol abuse. (Option A) Intravenous sodium bicarbonate administration is the preferred treatment for metformin-associated lactic acidosis. (Option B) Metformin can be given at a maximum 2550 mg/day dose in patients with increased blood glucose levels without demonstrating any adverse effects.   • Renal failure is common with metformin use.

Explanation:

In the management of an acute asthma exacerbation, the first-line treatment is a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) such as salbutamol (albuterol).

  • This medication works to relax bronchial smooth muscle, leading to rapid improvement in airway obstruction and relief of symptoms.

Inhaled corticosteroids (eg. fluticasone) and leukotriene receptor antagonists (eg. montelukast) (Options C & D) are used for long-term management and prevention of asthma symptoms and are not effective for immediate relief in an acute exacerbation.

Site
  • Labia majora is the most common (60%).

Presentation

Symptom

  • Cancer cachexia (weight loss and muscle wasting).

Vulvoscopy (Option A) is Limited to visual assessment; does not provide a definitive diagnosis.


Colposcopy (Option B) A valuable tool for visualizing and identifying suspicious areas for biopsy. However, it is not a diagnostic procedure on its own.

questions.stem: A 2 year old malnourished child is assessed using mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), and the measurement is 10 cm. What does this indicate?
questions.stemHtml: A 2 year old malnourished child is assessed using mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), and the measurement is 10 cm. What does this indicate?
questions.solution: g>Explanation: A MUAC measurement significantly below the recommended threshold (11.5 cm between 6 months to 5 years of age) typically indicates severe wasting . Wasting is a form of acute malnutrition where the child has a skinny appearance due to recent and severe weight loss. Therefore, a low MUAC strongly suggests severe wasting. MUAC is considered an age-independent measure for assessing malnutrition. Moderate Stunting (Option A): It is assessed using height-for-age measurements, which reflect long-term nutritional status and growth. MUAC is not used to diagnose stunting; thus, a low MUAC measurement would not indicate moderate stunting. Chronic Malnutrition (Option C): It is associated with long-term nutritional deficiencies and is evaluated through height-for-age measurements that show stunting. MUAC is more suited for detecting acute malnutrition rather than chronic malnutrition. Obesity (Option D) is identified through high BMI or weight-for-height measurements, not by a low MUAC. Since MUAC is used to assess acute malnutrition, it cannot indicate obesity. @Neet_pg_bot

g>Explanation:

A MUAC measurement significantly below the recommended threshold (11.5 cm between 6 months to 5 years of age) typically indicates severe wasting. MUAC is considered an age-independent measure for assessing malnutrition.

 

Moderate Stunting (Option A): It is assessed using height-for-age measurements, which reflect long-term nutritional status and growth. MUAC is not used to diagnose stunting; thus, a low MUAC measurement would not indicate moderate stunting.

 

Chronic Malnutrition (Option C): It is associated with long-term nutritional deficiencies and is evaluated through height-for-age measurements that show stunting. MUAC is more suited for detecting acute malnutrition rather than chronic malnutrition.

 

Obesity (Option D) is identified through high BMI or weight-for-height measurements, not by a low MUAC. Since MUAC is used to assess acute malnutrition, it cannot indicate obesity.

"7b1f175723169277719459db16938e">ocular cysticercosis as it can trigger an inflammatory response, potentially leading to vision loss.
 

PRAZIQUANTEL

MOA

Causes calcium ion influx into the tapeworm, resulting in paralysis, detachment from the intestine, and death.

At higher concentrations, it breaks down the tapeworm's outer layer.

Pharmacokinetics

Extensively metabolised in the liver (⇒ less bioavailability)

Uses

Highly effective for all human tapeworm infections, especially for T. solium cysticercosis, where larvae invade tissues like the muscles, and skin.

Adverse effects
  1. In neurocysticercosis, killing larval cysts in the brain can trigger inflammation, leading to seizures and ￪intracranial pressure.
  2. C/I in ocular cysticercosis due to the risk of intense inflammatory response, tissue damage, and vision loss

Levamisole (Option A)

  • Levamisole is an antiparasitic drug that is primarily used to treat ascariasis (2nd line drug) and ancylostomiasis.
  • MOA: Stimulates Nm receptor causing spastic paralysis. 
  • A low dose of levamisole is an immunostimulant; High dose: Immunosuppression → bone marrow suppression (agranulocytosis).
  • Used in the treatment of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.

Oxamniquine (Option B) is used primarily to treat schistosomiasis caused by Schistosoma mansoni but is ineffective for S. haematobium and S. japonicum infections.

Metrifonate (Option D) is used primarily to treat infections caused by Schistosoma haematobium.

questions.stemHtml:
Match the following vitamins with their respective functional assessment tests:
			1. Vitamin B1 (Thiamine)
			a) Measure urinary methylmalonic acid
			2. Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin)
			b) Measure transketolase activity in red blood cells
			3. Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine)
			c) Measure glutathione reductase activity in red blood cells
			4. Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin)
			d) Measure activation of red blood cell transaminases with pyridoxal phosphate
questions.solution: Vitamin B1 (Thiamin) → Transketolase Activity (b) Thiamin acts as a coenzyme for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway. Measuring transketolase activity in red blood cells after adding thiamin pyrophosphate helps assess thiamin status. Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin) → Glutathione Reductase Activity (c) Riboflavin functions as a coenzyme for glutathione reductase (FAD-dependent). Measuring glutathione reductase activity in RBCs helps assess riboflavin status. Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) → Activation of RBC Transaminases (d) Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is a coenzyme for transaminases in amino acid metabolism. Measuring activation of RBC transaminases after PLP supplementation assesses B6 status. Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) → Urinary Methylmalonic Acid (a) B12 is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase , which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. B12 deficiency leads to increased urinary methylmalonic acid , making it a reliable marker. Topic Discussion: Functional Assessment Tests of Vitamins Vitamin Functional Assessment Test Key Enzyme/Process Assessed Clinical Relevance Vitamin B1 (Thiamin) Transketolase activity in RBCs Transketolase (Pentose Phosphate Pathway) Reduced activity indicates thiamin deficiency (e.g., Beriberi, Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome) Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin) Glutathione reductase activity in RBCs Glutathione Reductase (FAD-dependent) Low activity suggests riboflavin deficiency, leading to oxidative stress disorders Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) RBC transaminase activity (after PLP addition) Aminotransferases (ALT, AST) Decreased enzyme activity suggests B6 deficiency, leading to neuropathy and anemia Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) Urinary methylmalonic acid measurement Methylmalonyl-CoA Mutase Elevated levels indicate B12 deficiency, which can cause megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy @Neet_pg_bot

• Vitamin B1 (Thiamin) → Transketolase Activity (b)

    • Thiamin acts as a coenzyme for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway.

    • Measuring transketolase activity in red blood cells after adding thiamin pyrophosphate helps assess thiamin status.

  • Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin) → Glutathione Reductase Activity (c)

    • Riboflavin functions as a coenzyme for glutathione reductase (FAD-dependent).

    • Measuring glutathione reductase activity in RBCs helps assess riboflavin status.

  • Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) → Activation of RBC Transaminases (d)

    • Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is a coenzyme for transaminases in amino acid metabolism.

    • Measuring activation of RBC transaminases after PLP supplementation assesses B6 status.

  • Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) → Urinary Methylmalonic Acid (a)

    • B12 is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA.

    • B12 deficiency leads to increased urinary methylmalonic acid, making it a reliable marker.

Topic Discussion: Functional Assessment Tests of Vitamins

Vitamin Functional Assessment Test Key Enzyme/Process Assessed Clinical Relevance
Vitamin B1 (Thiamin) Transketolase activity in RBCs Transketolase (Pentose Phosphate Pathway) Reduced activity indicates thiamin deficiency (e.g., Beriberi, Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome)
Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin) Glutathione reductase activity in RBCs Glutathione Reductase (FAD-dependent) Low activity suggests riboflavin deficiency, leading to oxidative stress disorders

questions.stem: A patient experiencing postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is undergoing resuscitation due to active bleeding. Laboratory tests have shown a critically low fibrinogen level. What is the recommended target fibrinogen level for patients with active bleeding during postpartum hemorrhage?
questions.stemHtml: A patient experiencing postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is undergoing resuscitation due to active bleeding. Laboratory tests have shown a critically low fibrinogen level. What is the recommended target fibrinogen level for patients with active bleeding during postpartum hemorrhage?
questions.solution: n class="customMeta" data-dictid="a137b7092a16927772025412d4ef05">fibrinogen level for patients with active bleeding during postpartum hemorrhage is >200 mg/dL. Laboratory Evaluation Description Routine Laboratory Tests Tests: Complete blood count (including platelet count), Type and crossmatch for multiple units of red blood cells, Coagulation studies (fibrinogen concentration, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time). Note: Hemoglobin levels drop by ~1 g/dL for every 500 mL of blood loss. Fibrinogen Measurement Fibrinogen levels drop earlier than other coagulation factors and are a sensitive indicator of ongoing blood loss. Normal Range: 350-650 mg/dL in pregnancy. Levels below 200 mg/dL are associated with severe PPH and higher morbidity/mortality. Target: Recommended to maintain fibrinogen levels >200 mg/dL, ideally >300 mg/dL in active bleeding. Viscoelastic Testing: TEG/ROTEM Thromboelastography (TEG) and rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM). Function: Assess global blood hemostasis by measuring clot development, stabilization, and dissolution. Usage: Effective for guiding plasma and coagulation product therapy. ROTEM Findings: FIBTEM A10 (Amplitude at 10 minutes) ≤17 mm is suggestive of low fibrinogen levels. Fibrin-based clot strength (FIBTEM) is an early indicator of bleeding severity. FIBTEM A5 <10 mm may indicate severe PPH. @Neet_pg_bot

Laboratory Evaluation

Description

Routine Laboratory Tests

Tests:

  • Complete blood count (including platelet count),
  • Type and crossmatch for multiple units of red blood cells,
  • Coagulation studies (fibrinogen concentration, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time).

Note: Hemoglobin levels drop by ~1 g/dL for every 500 mL of blood loss.

Fibrinogen Measurement
  • Fibrinogen levels drop earlier than other coagulation factors and are a sensitive indicator of ongoing blood loss.
  • Normal Range:
    • 350-650 mg/dL in pregnancy.
    • Levels below 200 mg/dL are associated with severe PPH and higher morbidity/mortality.
  • Target: Recommended to maintain fibrinogen levels >200 mg/dL, ideally >300 mg/dL in active bleeding.

Viscoelastic Testing:

TEG/ROTEM 

Thromboelastography (TEG) and rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM).

  • Function: Assess global blood hemostasis by measuring clot development, stabilization, and dissolution.
  • Usage: Effective for guiding plasma and coagulation product therapy.
  • ROTEM Findings:
    • FIBTEM A10 (Amplitude at 10 minutes) ≤17 mm is suggestive of low fibrinogen levels.
    • Fibrin-based clot strength (FIBTEM) is an early indicator of bleeding severity. FIBTEM A5 <10 mm may indicate severe PPH.

questions.solution: typically a marker of internal malignancy. It is the characteristic rash of early Lyme disease , caused by the tick-borne spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi . Erythema chronicum migrans (ECM): Occurs in about 90% of patients at the site of the tick bite . Appears 1–36 days after the bite (average: 9 days). Results from local spread of the spirochete , forming a ring-shaped lesion that enlarges at a rate of several centimeters per week . May be: Intensely erythematous or barely noticeable Flat or elevated at the center , periphery , or both Occasionally accompanied by slight scaling Target-like morphology may appear due to central clearing. Moderate burning or itching occurs in about one-third of cases. Without treatment, the lesion fades within a few weeks (range: 1 day to 14 months). Associated features may include regional lymphadenopathy and mild systemic symptoms . Necrolytic migratory erythema (Option A): Associated with : Glucagonoma (a rare pancreatic islet cell tumor). Clinical features: Extremely erythematous plaques Superficial epidermal necrosis Centrifugal spread Correctly associated with internal malignancy. Acanthosis nigricans (Option B): Can be a cutaneous marker of internal malignancy, most commonly gastric adenocarcinoma . Clinical features: Velvety, hyperpigmented plaques in skin folds (e.g., neck, axilla, groin) Also associated with insulin resistance and diabetes mellitus . Erythroderma (Option C): Defined as inflammation affecting >90% of the body surface area . Causes include: Psoriasis Malignancies : Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma > Hodgkin’s lymphoma Drugs : Phenytoin, carbamazepine, gold salts, lithium, phenylbutazone, cimetidine Inherited disorders : Ichthyosiform erythroderma, pityriasis rubra pilaris Other dermatoses : Pemphigus foliaceus, lichen planus, crusted scabies, dermatomyositis Also linked to internal malignancies , especially lymphomas @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
typically a marker of internal malignancy. It is the characteristic rash of early Lyme disease, caused by the tick-borne spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi.

Erythema chronicum migrans (ECM):

  • Occurs in about 90% of patients at the site of the tick bite.

  • Appears 1–36 days after the bite (average: 9 days).

  • Results from local spread of the spirochete, forming a ring-shaped lesion that enlarges at a rate of several centimeters per week.

  • May be:

    • Intensely erythematous or barely noticeable

    • Flat or elevated at the center, periphery, or both

    • Occasionally accompanied by slight scaling

  • Target-like morphology may appear due to central clearing.

  • Moderate burning or itching occurs in about one-third of cases.

  • Without treatment, the lesion fades within a few weeks (range: 1 day to 14 months).

  • Associated features may include regional lymphadenopathy and mild systemic symptoms.

 

Necrolytic migratory erythema (Option A):

  • Associated with: Glucagonoma (a rare pancreatic islet cell tumor).

  • Clinical features:

    • Extremely erythematous plaques

    • Superficial epidermal necrosis

    • Centrifugal spread

  • Correctly associated with internal malignancy.

 

 

Acanthosis nigricans (Option B):

  • Can be a cutaneous marker of internal malignancy, most commonly gastric adenocarcinoma.

  • Clinical features:

    • Velvety, hyperpigmented plaques in skin folds (e.g., neck, axilla, groin)

  • Also associated with insulin resistance and diabetes mellitus.

Erythroderma (Option C):

  • Defined as inflammation affecting >90% of the body surface area.

  • Causes include:

    • Psoriasis

    • Malignancies: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma > Hodgkin’s lymphoma

    • Drugs: Phenytoin, carbamazepine, gold salts, lithium, phenylbutazone, cimetidine

    • Inherited disorders: Ichthyosiform erythroderma, pityriasis rubra pilaris

    • Other dermatoses: Pemphigus foliaceus, lichen planus, crusted scabies, dermatomyositis

  • Also linked to internal malignancies, especially lymphomas

Confirmatory Tests for Blood Stains in Forensic Medicine Confirmatory tests are critical for identifying blood presence and origin in forensic investigations. Methods include chemical, immunological, and mass spectrometry techniques for reliable results. questions.solution: rong>testicular torsion In Deming’s sign, the affected testis is positioned high due to twisting and cremaster muscle spasm Testicular torsion: An emergency condition where the testis twists on its axis, compromising blood supply, potentially leading to gangrene within 12-24 hours Direction of Rotation Right Testis: Rotates clockwise Left Testis: Rotates counterclockwise Predisposing Factors Inversion of the Testis High Investment of Tunica Vaginalis Gap Between Testis and Epididymis Heavy Straining Features Age Group: Common in children and adolescents Symptoms: Sudden onset of pain in the scrotum, groin, and lower abdomen; vomiting due to pylorospasm Signs: Tenderness, redness, and edema of the scrotal skin Deming's Sign: Affected testis is positioned high due to twisting and cremaster muscle spasm Angell's Sign: Opposite testis lies horizontally due to the presence of mesorchium Investigations WBC Count: Elevated levels Doppler Study: To assess testicular artery pulsation Ultrasound Abdomen Treatment Emergency Exploration: Scrotum exploration and untwisting of the testis. The viability of the testis is checked. Fixation: If viable, the testis is fixed to the scrotal sac with 2-3 interrupted nonabsorbable sutures (Prolene). Timing: If surgery occurs within 12-24 hours, viability may be retained. Any delay can lead to gangrene, requiring orchidectomy. Orchidectomy Consideration: If in doubt, the testis can be retained temporarily, with orchidectomy postponed to assess viability. Postoperative Care: A repeat Doppler study confirms viability. The opposite testis should also be fixed to prevent torsion. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
rong>testicular torsion

In Deming’s sign, the affected testis is positioned high due to twisting and cremaster muscle spasm

 

Testicular torsion:

  • An emergency condition where the testis twists on its axis, compromising blood supply, potentially leading to gangrene within 12-24 hours

 

Direction of Rotation
  • Right Testis: Rotates clockwise
  • Left Testis: Rotates counterclockwise

Predisposing Factors
  • Inversion of the Testis
  • High Investment of Tunica Vaginalis
  • Gap Between Testis and Epididymis
  • Heavy Straining

Features
  • Age Group: Common in children and adolescents
  • Symptoms: Sudden onset of pain in the scrotum, groin, and lower abdomen; vomiting due to pylorospasm
  • Signs: Tenderness, redness, and edema of the scrotal skin
  • Deming's Sign: Affected testis is positioned high due to twisting and cremaster muscle spasm
  • Angell's Sign: Opposite testis lies horizontally due to the presence of mesorchium

Investigations
  • WBC Count: Elevated levels
  • Doppler Study: To assess testicular artery pulsation
  • Ultrasound Abdomen

Treatment
  • Emergency Exploration: Scrotum exploration and untwisting of the testis. The viability of the testis is checked.
  • Fixation: If viable, the testis is fixed to the scrotal sac with 2-3 interrupted nonabsorbable sutures (Prolene).
  • Timing: If surgery occurs within 12-24 hours, viability may be retained. Any delay can lead to gangrene, requiring orchidectomy.
  • Orchidectomy Consideration: If in doubt, the testis can be retained temporarily, with orchidectomy postponed to assess viability.
  • Postoperative Care: A repeat Doppler study confirms viability. The opposite testis should also be fixed to prevent torsion.

questions.solution: /strong> Explanation: The progressive muscle weakness, difficulty walking, and frequent falls starting at age 5 , along with calf hypertrophy, a positive Gower’s sign, and elevated creatine kinase , are classic findings of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) . Genetic testing confirms a dystrophin gene mutation leading to complete absence of dystrophin , which is a characteristic finding Becker Muscular Dystrophy (BMD) (Option B) also involves mutations in the dystrophin gene but usually presents later (adolescence or adulthood) with a slower progression and milder symptoms. Calf hypertrophy can be seen in both BMD and DMD, but the overall course and severity of BMD are milder. Emery-Dreifuss Muscular Dystrophy (EDMD) (Option C) often presents with early contractures, cardiac involvement (conduction defects, arrhythmias), and humeroperoneal muscle weakness. It does not typically involve calf hypertrophy and has a different pattern of muscle weakness compared to DMD. Facioscapulohumeral Muscular Dystrophy (FSHD) (Option D) primarily affects the muscles of the face, shoulders, and upper arms. It usually presents in adolescence or early adulthood with a distinct pattern of muscle weakness that spares the lower limbs until later stages. @Neet_pg_bot

The progressive muscle weakness, difficulty walking, and frequent falls starting at age 5, along with calf hypertrophy, a positive Gower’s sign, and elevated creatine kinase, are classic findings of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). Genetic testing confirms a dystrophin gene mutation leading to complete absence of dystrophin, which is a characteristic finding

Becker Muscular Dystrophy (BMD) (Option B) also involves mutations in the dystrophin gene but usually presents later (adolescence or adulthood) with a slower progression and milder symptoms. Calf hypertrophy can be seen in both BMD and DMD, but the overall course and severity of BMD are milder.

Emery-Dreifuss Muscular Dystrophy (EDMD) (Option C) often presents with early contractures, cardiac involvement (conduction defects, arrhythmias), and humeroperoneal muscle weakness. It does not typically involve calf hypertrophy and has a different pattern of muscle weakness compared to DMD.

Facioscapulohumeral Muscular Dystrophy (FSHD) (Option D) primarily affects the muscles of the face, shoulders, and upper arms. It usually presents in adolescence or early adulthood with a distinct pattern of muscle weakness that spares the lower limbs until later stages.

questions.stemHtml: A 3-year-old child presents with cyanosis and difficulty in breathing during physical exertion. On physical examination, the patient has a harsh systolic murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border. A chest X-ray is performed and it shows the following features. questions.solution: xplanation: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF): Most common cyanotic congenital heart defect Results from abnormal development of the ventricular septum during fetal growth. It is characterized by four main features: Right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction Ventricular septal defect (VSD) Overriding aorta Right ventricular hypertrophy Chest X-ray Imaging in TOF: The classic finding on a chest X-ray for TOF is the “boot-shaped” heart (also known as coeur en sabot ), caused by right ventricular hypertrophy leading to an upward tilt of the cardiac apex. There is often a concave main pulmonary artery and decreased pulmonary vascular markings , reflecting the reduced blood flow through the pulmonary arteries due to the RVOT obstruction. Some patients may also present with a right-sided aortic arch , which can be identified on the X-ray. In Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA) (Option A), the chest X-ray often shows an “egg-on-a-string” appearance , due to the narrow mediastinum and enlarged heart, which is distinct from the boot-shaped heart of TOF. Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (TAPVC) (Option C) , especially the supracardiac type, presents with a “snowman” or “figure-of-eight” appearance on chest X-ray. This is caused by the dilated vertical vein and superior vena cava. Pulmonary congestion is common in TAPVC due to the abnormal drainage of pulmonary veins. In Tricuspid Atresia (Option D) , there is a reduced size of the right ventricle, leading to a small or normal-sized heart on X-ray. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
xplanation:

Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF):

  • Most common cyanotic congenital heart defect
  • Results from abnormal development of the ventricular septum during fetal growth.

 

It is characterized by four main features:

  1. Right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction
  2. Ventricular septal defect (VSD)
  3. Overriding aorta
  4. Right ventricular hypertrophy

Chest X-ray Imaging in TOF:

  • The classic finding on a chest X-ray for TOF is the “boot-shaped” heart (also known as coeur en sabot), caused by right ventricular hypertrophy leading to an upward tilt of the cardiac apex. There is often a concave main pulmonary artery and decreased pulmonary vascular markings, reflecting the reduced blood flow through the pulmonary arteries due to the RVOT obstruction.
  • Some patients may also present with a right-sided aortic arch, which can be identified on the X-ray.

 

In Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA) (Option A), the chest X-ray often shows an “egg-on-a-string” appearance, due to the narrow mediastinum and enlarged heart, which is

distinct from the boot-shaped heart of TOF.

 

Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (TAPVC) (Option C), especially the supracardiac type, presents with a “snowman” or “figure-of-eight” appearance on chest X-ray. This is caused by the dilated vertical vein and superior vena cava. Pulmonary congestion is common in TAPVC due to the abnormal drainage of pulmonary veins.

 

In Tricuspid Atresia (Option D), there is a reduced size of the right ventricle, leading to a small or normal-sized heart on X-ray.

questions.solution: escribes meningitis and India ink stain is used to visualize the organism in this scenario. Organism: Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast and a common cause of meningitis in HIV/AIDS patients. Staining method: Capsule does not take up stains, so negative staining is used India ink stain (a negative stain) is specifically used to visualize the capsule surrounding Cryptococcus neoformans in CSF samples. Nigrosin stain is another example of negative stain. Any negative staining for diagnosis is performed on a CSF sample . In negative staining, the background gets stained dark while the capsule appears as a clear halo around yeast. In brain biopsy or a tissue sample, mucicarmine stain is used to highlight the capsule (stains capsule red) Cryptococcus meningitis treatment: Induction phase: Liposomal Amphotericin B with Flucytosine Consolidation and maintenance: Fluconazole (long-term prophylaxis in HIV patients) Gram stain (Option A) is used to classify bacteria into Gram-positive or Gram-negative. Acid-fast stain (Option C) is used primarily to identify Mycobacterium species. Giemsa stain (Option D) contains both acidic and basic dyes, which helps identify certain blood parasites and cellular components @Neet_pg_bot

rong>Explanation:

Schizoid Personality Disorder: Characterized by lifelong social withdrawal, emotional coldness, and lack of desire for social relationships. This patient fits the classic presentation with no psychosis or interest in forming close relationships.

Personality disorder: An enduring pattern of inner experience and behavior that deviates markedly from the expectations of the individual’s culture

  • Pervasive and inflexible
  • Onset in adolescence or early adult- hood
  • Stable over time
  • Ego-syntonic (i.e., acceptable to the ego)
  • Leads to distress or impairment

DSM-5 divides the disorders into three categories, or clusters: A, B, and C.

Cluster A Personality Disorders

Cluster A personality disorders are characterized by odd and aloof behavior, prone to develop psychosis. They include:

  • Paranoid Personality Disorder
  • Schizoid Personality Disorder
  • Schizotypal Personality Disorder

Disorder

Key Features

Diagnosis

Treatment

Paranoid Personality Disorder (Option C ruled out)
  • Pervasive distrust and suspiciousness of others
  • Hostility, irritability, anger
  • Difficulty with trust and intimacy
  • Cynical view of world
  • No fixed delusions (vs. delusional disorder)
  • No hallucinations or formal thought disorder (vs. schizophrenia)
  • No tumultuous relationships (vs. borderline personality disorder)
  • No history of antisocial behavior (vs. antisocial personality disorder)
  • Psychotherapy: Straightforward and honest therapist, avoid warmth or deep interpretation
  • Group therapy: Helpful for some, but poorly tolerated
  • Behavior therapy: Social skills training, may feel intrusive

Schizoid Personality Disorder (Option B)
  • Lifelong social withdrawal
  • Eccentric, isolated, and lonely
  • Introverted with a bland affect
  • No psychotic symptoms (vs. schizophrenia, delusional disorder)
  • More withdrawn and aloof (vs. paranoid personality disorder)
  • No dysphoric loneliness
  • Fewer past relationships, possible autistic reverie
  • No desire for social interaction (vs. avoidant personality disorder)
  • Psychotherapy: Build trust, encourage expression
  • Group therapy: May benefit, initial silence likely
  • Pharmacotherapy: Limited evidence, medications for specific symptoms (e.g., emotional detachment)

Schizotypal Personality Disorder (Option A ruled out)
  • Social difficulties
  • Eccentric behavior and thinking (“magical thinking”)
  • Peculiar speech, superstitious beliefs, perceptual illusions
  • Odd behavior, thinking, and perception (vs. schizoid and avoidant personality disorders)
  • Differentiated from autism by the severity of language disorder
  • Lacks psychosis, or it's brief (vs. schizophrenia)
  • No odd behavior (vs. paranoid personality disorder)
  • Psychotherapy: Sensitive approach to avoid ridicule
  • Antipsychotics: Manage illusions and odd ideas
  • Antidepressants: Used for depressive symptoms

Avoidant Personality Disorder (Option D): Involves social withdrawal due to fear of rejection, but those individuals still desire social connections, unlike schizoid personality disorder (Cluster C Personality Disorder).

questions.solution: ng> Explanation: This patient has an unruptured ectopic pregnancy in the right fallopian tube that has failed to respond to medical management with methotrexate. Laparoscopic salpingectomy involves the removal of the affected fallopian tube . It is indicated when medical therapy fails or is contraindicated, such as in cases of larger ectopic pregnancies (> 4 cm) or persistent beta hCG levels. Expectant management (Option A) involves observation of the patient, hoping for spontaneous resolution. This is a viable option in cases where the beta hCG level is low or falling. Hysterectomy (Option B) is not considered a management option for ectopic pregnancy. Laparoscopic linear salpingostomy (Option C) is done only in H/O infertility or if the unaffected tube is also looking unhealthy. @Neet_pg_bot

Toxicological Analysis in Suspected Poisoning Cases Toxicological analysis is essential for confirming or excluding poisoning as a cause of illness or death. It involves various specimens, tests, and result interpretations. Specimens for Analysis Specimen Importance Blood Primary specimen; collect from femoral, iliac, or axillary veins to avoid contamination. (Option A ruled out) Preservative: Lithium heparin or EDTA tube, fluoride/oxalate, if alcohol is suspected Urine Useful for detecting parent compounds and metabolites of poisons. (Option B ruled out) Preservative: No preservative, sodium fluoride is added, if alcohol is suspected Gastric Contents Helps identify ingested poisons and their concentrations through vomitus and stomach contents analysis. Preservative: Saturated salt solution if there is no chance of acid poison. Rectified spirit if poisoned by acid. Liver Analyzes metabolism and concentration of drugs; critical when blood/urine concentrations are low. Bile can detect specific substances like chlorpromazine and morphine. (Option D ruled out) Preservative: Saturated salt solution if there is no chance of acid poison. Rectified spirit if poisoned by acid. Hair and Nails Detects heavy metal poisoning; metals accumulate in keratin. Neutron activation analysis identifies specific metals and exposure patterns. (Option C) Scene Residues Provides clues about the poison through materials found at the scene, such as tablets or empty containers. Types of Toxicological Tests Test Type Description Qualitative Tests Determine presence/absence of specific drugs or toxins; positive indicates presence, negative suggests absence or low concentration. Quantitative Tests Measure specific concentration of drugs or toxins; crucial for assessing severity of toxicity for substances like acetaminophen, alcohols, barbiturates, and heavy metals. Interpretation of Results Negative Results : A negative result does not exclude poisoning; it may indicate the substance was undetectable or below detection limits. Retesting may yield a positive result. Quantitative Analysis : Interpretation depends on ingestion timing, individual metabolism, and possible drug interactions. @Neet_pg_bot

Toxicological analysis is essential for confirming or excluding poisoning as a cause of illness or death. It involves various specimens, tests, and result interpretations.

Specimen

Types of Toxicological Tests

Test Type

Description

Qualitative Tests

Determine presence/absence of specific drugs or toxins; positive indicates presence, negative suggests absence or low concentration.

Quantitative Tests

Measure specific concentration of drugs or toxins; crucial for assessing severity of toxicity for substances like acetaminophen, alcohols, barbiturates, and heavy metals.

Interpretation of Results

  • Negative Results: A negative result does not exclude poisoning; it may indicate the substance was undetectable or below detection limits. Retesting may yield a positive result.
  • Quantitative Analysis: Interpretation depends on ingestion timing, individual metabolism, and possible drug interactions.

The parents give vague explanations and claim the child "bruises easily." A CT scan reveals subdural hematoma without a clear trauma history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: or Battered Baby Syndrome is strongly suggested when a child presents with multiple injuries at different stages of healing, and the parents provide a vague or inconsistent explanation. The rib fractures, bruises, and a healing burn- combined with intracranial hemorrhage without significant trauma- point to ongoing physical abuse. Battered Baby Syndrome (Caffey-Kempe Syndrome): A battered child is one who has sustained repeated physical harm due to intentional violence inflicted by a parent or guardian. Other names include Caffey-Kempe syndrome , maltreatment syndrome , or parent-infant traumatic stress syndrome . Features Raising Suspicion of Abuse: Inconsistent History : Parents may provide vague explanations for injuries, such as a fall, which do not match the type or timing of the injuries. Delayed Medical Care : Parents often seek medical help only when the child’s condition worsens. Injuries in Various Stages : Multiple injuries at different healing stages are often present. Parental Admission : Parents may later confess to mild punishment but downplay the severity. Injuries: Surface Injuries : Bruises, abrasions, and lacerations, including characteristic labial frenulum tears. CNS Injuries : Encephalopathy, retinal hemorrhages, and subdural hematoma (SDH), indicative of shaken baby syndrome. Eye Injuries : Retinal hemorrhages and possible lens dislocation. Visceral Injuries : Damage to the spleen, liver, or intestines. Burns : Cigarette burns or scalds from hot liquids are often found. Skeletal Injuries : Fractures (transverse, spiral, metaphyseal chip fractures), rib fractures, and the characteristic "string of beads" appearance on X-rays are common. Cardiovascular Injuries : Rib fractures, lung and heart contusions. Genitourinary Injuries : Consider sexual abuse. Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option A) : Causes frequent fractures but does not account for bruising, burns, or intracranial hemorrhage. Munchausen syndrome by proxy (Option C) : Involves a caregiver fabricating or inducing illness in a child, but the repeated physical injuries in this case make direct physical abuse more likely. Hemophilia (Option D) : Could explain bruising but not the presence of fractures and burn marks. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male was admitted to the ICU after a motorcycle accident with a femur fracture 24 hours ago. He is confused, has a petechial rash, tachycardia (HR 120), tachypnea (RR 28), and an oxygen saturation of 65%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old male was admitted to the ICU after a motorcycle accident with a femur fracture 24 hours ago. He is confused, has a petechial rash, tachycardia (HR 120), tachypnea (RR 28), and an oxygen saturation of 65%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Meta" data-dictid="1c07a1135f1692777187f547678386">Embolism due to the combination of confusion, petechial rash, tachycardia, tachypnea, and low oxygen saturation following a femur fracture. Fat Embolism Fat embolism is a multi-organ disorder caused by fat globules entering the bloodstream, commonly occurring after high-risk orthopedic injuries, particularly femur fractures. Classic Triad Hypoxia Petechiae Altered mental status Other Symptoms Tachycardia, fever, anemia, thrombocytopenia, pulmonary dysfunction (e.g., tachypnea, respiratory acidosis). Etiology Young adults (20-30 years): Long bone fractures Iatrogenic cause: Occurs after reamed intramedullary (IM) nailing of the femur. Pathogenesis Following injury, fat from bone marrow or platelet agglutination enters injured vessels and travels as emboli, leading to various clinical manifestations. Investigation Chest X-ray: Snowstorm appearance (pathognomonic). PaO₂ <60 mm Hg. Platelet count <1.5 lakhs. ECG: Prominent S-wave Other lab findings: Anemia, hypocalcemia. CT scan and MRI: Assess severity. Management Respiratory support: Oxygen or ventilator support to restore PaO₂. Drug therapy: Steroids: Reduce lung inflammation and improve gas exchange. Heparin: Lipolytic and antiplatelet agent. Low molecular weight dextran: Increases plasma volume. Antibiotics and other supportive care. Definitive fracture treatment: Early fixation to prevent worsening. Pulmonary Embolism (Option B) typically presents with sudden onset dyspnea, chest pain, and tachycardia, but lacks the petechial rash and altered mental status seen in this case. Additionally, the patient's history of femur fracture points more strongly to fat embolism rather than pulmonary embolism. Deep Vein Thrombosis (Option C) typically presents with pain, swelling, and redness in the affected limb, but lacks the petechial rash, altered mental status, and respiratory symptoms seen in fat embolism, making DVT less likely in this case. Pneumothorax (Option D) presents with pleuritic chest pain and absent breath sounds, which differs from the petechial rash and altered mental status seen in fat embolism, especially after femur fractures. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Meta" data-dictid="1c07a1135f1692777187f547678386">Embolism due to the combination of confusion, petechial rash, tachycardia, tachypnea, and low oxygen saturation following a femur fracture.

 

Fat Embolism

Fat embolism is a multi-organ disorder caused by fat globules entering the bloodstream, commonly occurring after high-risk orthopedic injuries, particularly femur fractures.

Classic Triad
  • Hypoxia
  • Petechiae
  • Altered mental status

Other Symptoms

Tachycardia, fever, anemia, thrombocytopenia, pulmonary dysfunction (e.g., tachypnea, respiratory acidosis).

Etiology
  • Young adults (20-30 years): Long bone fractures
  • Iatrogenic cause: Occurs after reamed intramedullary (IM) nailing of the femur.

Pathogenesis

Following injury, fat from bone marrow or platelet agglutination enters injured vessels and travels as emboli, leading to various clinical manifestations.

Investigation
  • Chest X-ray: Snowstorm appearance (pathognomonic).

 

  • PaO₂ <60 mm Hg.
  • Platelet count <1.5 lakhs.
  • ECG: Prominent S-wave
  • Other lab findings: Anemia, hypocalcemia.
  • CT scan and MRI: Assess severity.

Management

  • Respiratory support: Oxygen or ventilator support to restore PaO₂.
  • Drug therapy:
    • Steroids: Reduce lung inflammation and improve gas exchange.
    • Heparin: Lipolytic and antiplatelet agent.
    • Low molecular weight dextran: Increases plasma volume.
    • Antibiotics and other supportive care.
  • Definitive fracture treatment: Early fixation to prevent worsening.

 

Pulmonary Embolism (Option B) typically presents with sudden onset dyspnea, chest pain, and tachycardia, but lacks the petechial rash and altered mental status seen in this case. Additionally, the patient's history of femur fracture points more strongly to fat embolism rather than pulmonary embolism.

 

Deep Vein Thrombosis (Option C) typically presents with pain, swelling, and redness in the affected limb, but lacks the petechial rash, altered mental status, and respiratory symptoms seen in fat embolism, making DVT less likely in this case.

 

Pneumothorax (Option D) presents with pleuritic chest pain and absent breath sounds, which differs from the petechial rash and altered mental status seen in fat embolism, especially after femur fractures.

Which is the best time to perform an endometrial biopsy to diagnose endometrial tuberculosis?
questions.stemHtml:
A 29-year-old woman presents with complaints of infertility and chronic lower abdominal pain for the past year. She mentions recent unintentional weight loss and occasional night sweats. Her menstrual cycles have been regular, but she has experienced heavier-than-usual periods over the past six months. Considering her symptoms and clinical history, the clinician suspects endometrial tuberculosis and decides to perform an endometrial biopsy for diagnosis.
Which is the best time to perform an endometrial biopsy to diagnose endometrial tuberculosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Any time during the menstrual cycle

questions.solution: The optimal time to perform an endometrial biopsy for diagnosing endometrial tuberculosis is during the late premenstrual phase of the menstrual cycle. The tubercle is found in the basal layer of the endometrium and moves to the surface before menstruation. Following the shedding of the endometrium during menstruation, reinfection arises from the basal layer lesions or the fallopian tubes. Layers affected: Endometrial tuberculosis typically affects the endometrial layer (60%) while sparing the myometrium. Endometrial biopsy is done during the premenstrual period by D&C or hysteroscopy directed biopsy. Menstrual blood collected on the first day of menstruation (superficial layer is shed off) can also be used as a diagnostic sample because it may contain the bacilli responsible for the infection. @Neet_pg_bot

Hydrops is diagnosed by identifying two or more fetal effusions – pleural, pericardial, or ascites – or one effusion plus anasarca. Pathophysiology of hydrops fetalis: Congenital Anemia of the Newborn (Option A) is the mildest form of HDFN , characterized by slow destruction of RBCs in the first few weeks of life, leading to anemia, enlarged liver, and spleen, but typically without noticeable jaundice. Arteriovenous Fistula (AVF)

  • AVF is a communication between an artery and a vein that may be either congenital or acquired (trauma or surgical).
  • Structurally, they are arterialised (become dilated, tortuous and thick-walled).

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is true about the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle?

options.label: A
options.text: It involves the formation of citrulline from ornithine.

options.label: B
options.text: It is catalysed by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I).

options.label: C
options.text: It is regulated by argininosuccinate synthetase.

options.label: D
options.text: It is controlled by the enzyme argininosuccinate lyase.

questions.answerText: It is catalysed by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I).
questions.solution: b4c">phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) reaction is the rate-limiting step in the urea cycle. The urea cycle is a cycle of biochemical reactions that produce urea from ammonia. It is also known as the Krebs-Henseleit urea cycle or the Ornithine cycle. It starts in the mitochondria of hepatocytes and ends in the cytoplasm . Reactions in the Urea Cycle Step Reaction Details Enzyme Involved and Location Key Points Carbamoyl Phosphate Formation Formation of carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia and CO₂ using ATP. Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I (CPS I) Mitochondria The rate-limiting step of the urea cycle. Irreversible and allosterically regulated by N-acetyl glutamate (NAG). Citrulline Formation (Option A) Transfer of carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine to form citrulline. Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC) Mitochondria Citrulline moves from mitochondria to cytosol for further processing in the urea cycle. Argininosuccinate Formation (Option C) Citrulline combines with aspartate to form argininosuccinate. Argininosuccinate Synthetase Cytoplasm Requires ATP. Links the urea cycle with the TCA cycle via aspartate. Argininosuccinate Cleavage (Option D) Cleavage of argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate. Argininosuccinate Lyase Cytoplasm Fumarate enters the TCA cycle, providing a connection between the urea cycle and other metabolic pathways. Arginine Cleavage to Ornithine and Urea Hydrolysis of arginine to produce ornithine and urea. Arginase Cytoplasm Ornithine is recycled back into the urea cycle. Urea is excreted by the kidneys, with some urea also entering the intestine. Fate of Urea Urea is transported to the kidneys, filtered, and excreted in urine. Kidneys/ Intestine Urea excretion is the final step, removing excess nitrogen from the body. @Neet_pg_bot

b4c">phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) reaction is the rate-limiting step in the urea cycle.
  • The urea cycle is a cycle of biochemical reactions that produce urea from ammonia.
  • It is also known as the Krebs-Henseleit urea cycle or the Ornithine cycle.
  • It starts in the mitochondria of hepatocytes and ends in the cytoplasm.

    •  

                         

     

    Reactions in the Urea Cycle

    Step

    Reaction Details

    Enzyme Involved and Location

    Key Points

    Carbamoyl Phosphate Formation
    • Formation of carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia and CO₂ using ATP.
    • Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I (CPS I)
     
    • Mitochondria
    • The rate-limiting step of the urea cycle.
    • Irreversible and allosterically regulated by N-acetyl glutamate (NAG).

    Citrulline Formation (Option A)
    • Transfer of carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine to form citrulline.
    • Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC)
       
    • Mitochondria
    • Citrulline moves from mitochondria to cytosol for further processing in the urea cycle.

    Argininosuccinate Formation (Option C)
    • Citrulline combines with aspartate to form argininosuccinate.
    • Argininosuccinate Synthetase
     
    • Cytoplasm
    • Requires ATP.
    • Links the urea cycle with the TCA cycle via aspartate.

    Argininosuccinate Cleavage (Option D)
    • Cleavage of argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate.
    • Argininosuccinate Lyase
     
    • Cytoplasm
    • Fumarate enters the TCA cycle, providing a connection between the urea cycle and other metabolic pathways.

    Arginine Cleavage to Ornithine and Urea
    • Hydrolysis of arginine to produce ornithine and urea.
    • Arginase
     
    • Cytoplasm
    • Ornithine is recycled back into the urea cycle.
    • Urea is excreted by the kidneys, with some urea also entering the intestine.

    Fate of Urea
    • Urea is transported to the kidneys, filtered, and excreted in urine.
    • Kidneys/ Intestine
    • Urea excretion is the final step, removing excess nitrogen from the body.

questions.stemHtml: A 10-year-old schoolboy was playing on the monkey bars during recess when he suddenly slipped and fell onto his outstretched hand. He immediately felt intense pain in his wrist. On examination, there is significant swelling and tenderness over the wrist. An X-ray of the wrist reveals specific findings indicative of a fracture. Based on the history, clinical features, and X-ray findings, what is the most likely diagnosis? {{caption_text}}
questions.solution: Explanation: 10-year-old boy who fell onto an outstretched hand, a common mechanism for wrist injuries in children. The intense pain he experienced immediately after the fall aligns with this type of injury. The X-ray findings show a subtle bulging of the cortex in the distal radius without a visible fracture line, which is characteristic of a torus fracture. This injury occurs due to the flexibility of pediatric bones, resulting in compression rather than a complete break. Torus (buckle) fractures Definition Torus fractures, also known as buckle fractures, occur when the periosteum (the outer layer of the bone) buckles or compresses, typically due to axial loading forces. This type of fracture is incomplete. Common Sites Most frequently affects long bones, especially the tibia (particularly the lower end near the metaphysis, where bones are more spongy and susceptible to compression). The radius is another common site, particularly in falls involving outstretched hands (FOOSH injuries). Clinical Features There is minimal swelling and pain over the affected site. Unlike complete fractures, there is no visible bone displacement. Diagnosis Radiographs show a subtle buckling of the cortex, but there is no break in bone continuity. The imaging may require careful interpretation to differentiate from complete fractures. Treatment Immobilization with a plaster of Paris (POP) slab for 4–5 weeks is usually sufficient. Surgery is not needed, as these fractures typically heal well with conservative treatment. Follow-up may include monitoring for any signs of healing or complications. Avulsion fracture (Option A): This occurs when a small piece of bone is pulled off by a ligament or tendon. It is less likely in this scenario, which involves a fall on an outstretched hand and not a joint injury. Impacted fracture (Option B): This occurs when the broken ends of the bone are driven into each other. It would typically show more bone disruption, which is not seen here. Greenstick fracture (Option D): This fracture is also common in children and involves a partial break of the bone, where one side breaks and the other bends. It typically presents with a more visible fracture line compared to the subtle bulging seen in a torus fracture. @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation:

 

  • 10-year-old boy who fell onto an outstretched hand, a common mechanism for wrist injuries in children.
  • The intense pain he experienced immediately after the fall aligns with this type of injury.
  • The X-ray findings show a subtle bulging of the cortex in the distal radius without a visible fracture line, which is characteristic of a torus fracture.
  • This injury occurs due to the flexibility of pediatric bones, resulting in compression rather than a complete break.
Torus (buckle) fractures

Definition

Torus fractures, also known as buckle fractures, occur when the periosteum (the outer layer of the bone) buckles or compresses, typically due to axial loading forces. This type of fracture is incomplete.


 

Common Sites
  • Most frequently affects long bones, especially the tibia (particularly the lower end near the metaphysis, where bones are more spongy and susceptible to compression).
  • The radius is another common site, particularly in falls involving outstretched hands (FOOSH injuries).

Clinical Features
  • There is minimal swelling and pain over the affected site.
  • Unlike complete fractures, there is no visible bone displacement.

Diagnosis

Radiographs show a subtle buckling of the cortex, but there is no break in bone continuity. The imaging may require careful interpretation to differentiate from complete fractures.

Treatment
  • Immobilization with a plaster of Paris (POP) slab for 4–5 weeks is usually sufficient.
  • Surgery is not needed, as these fractures typically heal well with conservative treatment. Follow-up may include monitoring for any signs of healing or complications.

Avulsion fracture (Option A):

  • This occurs when a small piece of bone is pulled off by a ligament or tendon.
  • It is less likely in this scenario, which involves a fall on an outstretched hand and not a joint injury.

Impacted fracture (Option B):

  • This occurs when the broken ends of the bone are driven into each other.
  • It would typically show more bone disruption, which is not seen here.

Greenstick fracture (Option D):

  • This fracture is also common in children and involves a partial break of the bone, where one side breaks and the other bends.
  • It typically presents with a more visible fracture line compared to the subtle bulging seen in a torus fracture.

questions.stem: According to the system, which has the logo below and under the Central Birth and Death Registration Act, 1969, what is the time limit for registering for birth and death events in India?
questions.stemHtml: According to the system, which has the logo below and under the Central Birth and Death Registration Act, 1969, what is the time limit for registering for birth and death events in India?
questions.solution: Explanation: The logo represents the Civil Registration System (Aka Vital Survey of the country) under the Central Births and Deaths Registration Act of 1969, which came into force on April 1st, 1970. The flame represents birth and the circle represents death. According to this system: Registration of birth and death is compulsory throughout the nation The public reports events occurring in their household, while heads of institutions, such as nursing homes, hotels, and jails, report events occurring in their institutes. The time limit for registering the event of birth and death in India is 21 days. For NRI, the time limit is 90 days. Default leads to a late fee. Since 2018, an Aadhaar number has been a must for registration for Death. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient has a history of vesicles and bullae , which later ruptured to form vegetative erosions in intertriginous areas- supporting the diagnosis. Pemphigus Vegetans: A variant of pemphigus vulgaris , characterized by vegetating plaques . Flexural involvement is typical- especially in areas like groin, axillae, inframammary region. Pemphigus foliaceus (Option A) Crusted erosions in seborrheic areas (face, chest, scalp); no mucosal involvement; superficial blistering. questions.solutionHtml:
ign:center">
  • The image shows moist, vegetative, hypertrophic plaques located in a flexural region, which is characteristic of pemphigus vegetans.
     
  • The patient has a history of vesicles and bullae, which later ruptured to form vegetative erosions in intertriginous areas- supporting the diagnosis.
     
  • This is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris, often misdiagnosed without considering the specific morphology and location of lesions.
     

Pemphigus Vegetans:

  • A variant of pemphigus vulgaris, characterized by vegetating plaques.
     
  • Flexural involvement is typical- especially in areas like groin, axillae, inframammary region.
     
  • Develops after bullae or pustules rupture, leading to:
     
    • Hypertrophic, granulating, exudative erosions.
       
    • Lesions may become foul-smelling and infected.
       
  • Oral mucosa may be involved:
     
    • Cerebriform tongue (called Premlata sign)

 

 

  • Two subtypes:
     
    • Neumann type – more severe, vesiculobullous onset.
    • Hallopeau type – milder, pustular onset leading to vegetative growth.

Differential Diagnoses:

Diagnosis

Key Features

Pemphigus vegetans (Option D)

Vegetating erosions in flexures; post-vesicular phase; cerebriform tongue (Premlata sign); Neumann/Hallopeau types.

Pemphigus foliaceus (Option A)

Crusted erosions in seborrheic areas (face, chest, scalp); no mucosal involvement; superficial blistering.

Endemic PF (fogo selvagem) (Option B)

Seen in rural Brazil/Colombia; associated with black fly bites (Simulium); affects children/young adults.

Condyloma acuminata (Option C)

HPV-related genital warts; soft, pink, verrucous or filiform lesions; no vesicle-bullae history.

Condyloma lata (secondary syphilis)

Flat, moist, broad-based lesions in groin/perineum; painless; seen in syphilis- not relevant here.

 

Pemphigus foliaceus (Option A):
 

  • Incorrect because it causes crusted erosions in seborrheic areas, not vegetative plaques in flexures.
  • Mucosal involvement is absent.

 

Endemic pemphigus foliaceus (Option B):
 

  • Incorrect as it occurs in endemic regions (e.g., Brazil), often in young populations living near black fly–infested rivers.
  • Not associated with vegetative or hypertrophic lesions.

Condyloma acuminata (Option C):
 

  • Incorrect as these are genital warts caused by HPV.
  • Present as verrucous or filiform growths, not hypertrophic vegetating plaques.
  • Condyloma lata, seen in secondary syphilis, are broad-based, flat, moist lesions that typically occur in the intertriginous areas such as the groin and perianal region.
